content.topicNotes: 3D Printers What is a 3D printer A 3D printer is an output device that creates physical objects from digital models. 3D printing is an example of additive manufacturing. Additive manufacturing builds objects layer by layer. Subtractive manufacturing removes material to shape an object. A digital model is required before printing begins. How 3D printers work The digital model is sliced into thin layers by software. The printer deposits material layer by layer. Direct printing extrudes material through a nozzle. Direct printing pushes melted material out to form layers. Binder printing joins powdered material using a liquid binder. Binder printing sprays a binding agent onto powder. Uses of 3D printers Engineers use 3D printers to create prototypes quickly. Schools use 3D printers in design and technology lessons. Doctors produce medical models and prosthetics. Manufacturers create custom parts and tools. Hobbyists design and print personalised objects. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of 3D printing Complex shapes can be produced easily. Additive manufacturing reduces material waste. Rapid prototyping speeds up product development. Disadvantages of 3D printing Printing can be slow for large objects. 3D printers can be expensive to purchase and maintain. Available materials may be limited compared to traditional manufacturing.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Input & Output

content.topicNotes: 3G, 4G & Infra-red 3G 3G stands for third generation mobile network. It lets mobile devices send and receive data over a wide area. 3G supports web browsing, email, and video calls. It is slower than 4G. Typical download speeds are around 1-8 Mbps (megabits per second). 4G 4G stands for fourth generation mobile network. It is faster than 3G. Typical download speeds are around 10-50 Mbps. 4G supports high-definition video streaming and fast web browsing. It covers large areas and works with smartphones and tablets. Infra-red (IR) Infra-red (IR) uses invisible light waves to send data. It works only over very short distances. The two devices must point directly at each other. TV remote controls use IR to send signals to a TV. IR cannot pass through walls or solid objects. Comparing the Types 3G and 4G work over long distances using radio waves. IR works only over very short distances using light. 4G is the fastest of the three types. 3G is slower but still covers wide areas. IR is the slowest and most limited in range.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Types of Digital Communications

content.topicNotes: Accessibility Devices What are Accessibility Devices? Accessibility devices are digital devices that help people with disabilities use computers. They are peripheral devices. A peripheral device connects to a computer to add extra features. They meet particular needs that standard devices cannot. Braille Displays A Braille display is an output device for people who are blind or have low vision. It converts on-screen text into Braille. Braille is a system of raised dots that represent letters and numbers. The user reads the dots with their fingertips. Braille Keyboards A Braille keyboard is an input device for blind or visually impaired users. The keys are labelled with raised Braille dots. The user feels the dots to find the correct key. It lets them type without needing to see the keyboard. Braille Printers A Braille printer is an output device that prints text as raised Braille dots on paper. It is also called an embosser. It lets blind users read printed documents with their fingertips. It replaces a standard inkjet or laser printer for this purpose. Haptic Feedback and Vibration Devices Haptic feedback devices send physical sensations to the user. Haptic means relating to the sense of touch. Vibration alerts replace sounds or visual signals. They help users who are deaf or hard of hearing. A vibrating phone alert is a common example. Reading Pens A reading pen is a handheld input device. The user scans printed text by sliding the pen across a page. The pen reads the text aloud through a speaker or earphone. It helps users with dyslexia or visual impairments. It can also give word definitions on a small screen.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > ICT systems to meet specified needs

content.topicNotes: Accessibility Software What is Accessibility Software? Accessibility software helps users with disabilities use a computer. It makes tasks easier for people who struggle with standard input or output. Choosing the right software depends on the user's specific needs. For example, a user with poor vision needs different software than a user who cannot type. Voice Recognition Software Voice recognition software turns spoken words into text or commands. The computer listens through a microphone and acts on what it hears. It helps users who find typing difficult or painful. A user can dictate a document or control the computer by speaking. Dragon NaturallySpeaking is a well-known example. Magnification Tools Magnification tools make items on the screen appear larger. This helps users with visual impairments see text and images more clearly. The tool zooms into part of the screen, like a digital magnifying glass. Windows Magnifier is a built-in example found on most PCs. Choosing the Right Software The right accessibility software must match the user's needs. A user who cannot speak should not rely on voice recognition software. A user with good vision may not need magnification tools. Always check what the user struggles with before choosing a solution.

content.topicNotes: Actuators What is an actuator An actuator (or control device) is an output device that causes a physical action. It converts electrical signals from a computer into movement. Actuators control mechanical systems. They are used in automated and control systems. Actuators do not produce visual or audio output. Types of actuators Electric motors are actuators that produce rotational movement. A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. Solenoids are actuators that create linear movement. Linear movement is movement in a straight line. Relays act as switches controlled by electrical signals. Uses of actuators Actuators are used in automatic doors to open and close. Washing machines use actuators to rotate the drum. Heating systems use actuators to control valves. Robots use actuators to move arms and wheels. Traffic lights use actuators to control signals. Advantages and disadvantages An advantage is that actuators enable automatic control of systems. An advantage is reduced need for human intervention. A disadvantage is that actuators require power to operate. A disadvantage is that mechanical parts can wear out. Faulty actuators may cause system failure.

content.topicNotes: Adjusting Brightness and Contrast Understanding Brightness Users adjust brightness to control the overall lightness or darkness of an image. Brightness: the relative intensity of light emitted or reflected by an image. Reducing brightness helps correct an overexposed photo to make it look more natural. Overexposed: a term for an image that is too bright because it was exposed to too much light. Increasing brightness makes a dark or underexposed image much easier to see. Adjusting Contrast Users modify contrast to change the difference between the darkest and lightest parts of a graphic. Contrast: the scale of difference between the blackest shadows and the whitest highlights in an image. High contrast makes shadows darker and highlights brighter, creating a more dramatic and vivid look. Low contrast reduces the difference between tones, making the image appear flatter or more grey. Practical ICT Applications Designers balance brightness and contrast to ensure that image details remain visible during the printing process. Poorly adjusted images may hide important features in very dark shadows or very bright highlights. Technicians often use these tools to enhance scanned documents or low-quality photographs for school publications. Accurate adjustments help maintain the professional standard required for ICT project portfolios.

content.topicNotes: Advantages and Disadvantages of Computer Types Desktop computers Desktop computers are designed for use at a fixed location. Advantages Desktop computers offer high performance for demanding tasks. Internal components can be easily upgraded or replaced. Disadvantages Desktop computers are not portable. A fixed workspace and mains power supply are required. Laptop computers Laptop computers are portable computers with built-in components. Advantages A laptop computer can be used in different locations. A rechargeable battery allows use without mains power. Disadvantages Hardware upgrades are limited. Battery life restricts usage time. Smartphones Smartphones are handheld computers with mobile network connectivity. Advantages Smartphones combine communication and computing features. A wide range of apps is available for different tasks. Disadvantages Small screens limit productivity. Smartphones are less powerful than laptops or desktop computers. Tablets and phablets Tablets and phablets are portable touch-screen computers. Advantages Touch screens provide intuitive interaction. Battery life is usually longer than laptops. Disadvantages Typing long documents is difficult using on-screen keyboards. Professional software support is limited.

content.topicNotes: Advantages for Organisations Improved Communication The internet has improved the way organisations communicate. Emails, video calls and instant messaging let staff talk quickly. These tools work across the world in seconds. Faster communication means quicker decisions. Teams in different locations can work together easily. Access to Global Markets A global market means selling to customers anywhere in the world. The internet lets organisations reach these customers online. A website or app can take orders from any country. This was very hard to do before the internet. Small businesses can now compete with large ones worldwide. Access to a Global Workforce The internet lets organisations hire staff from anywhere in the world. This is called a global workforce. Workers can do their jobs remotely using computers and the internet. Video calls and shared files let remote teams work together. Organisations can find the best person for a job, no matter where they live. Changes in Information Management The internet has changed how organisations store and use information. Large amounts of data can be stored digitally in databases. A database is an organised collection of electronic records. Information can be searched, sorted and shared very quickly. This makes it easier to spot trends and make good decisions. Changes in How Information is Used Organisations use data to improve their services. For example, a shop can track what sells well and order more stock. Reports and charts can be made from data in seconds. Sharing information across departments is faster and easier. Better use of information helps organisations work more efficiently.

content.topicNotes: Align Headers, Footers, and Tab Stops Default Tab Stops Word processors insert predefined tab stops automatically inside headers and footers. Tab stops are preset horizontal positions where the text cursor moves when you press the Tab key. The system sets a center tab stop in the middle of the margin boundaries. The system configures a right tab stop precisely at the right margin line. Modifying page margins requires updating header and footer tab stops to ensure right-aligned items remain aligned. Header and footer content must stay within the set page limits and avoid colliding with the body text. Three-Part Alignment Users achieve three separate alignments on a single line using default tab stops. Alignment refers to the positioning of text relative to the page margins. Left-aligned text starts immediately at the left margin without pressing Tab. Centered text requires the user to press the Tab key once. Right-aligned text requires the user to press the Tab key a second time. Custom Tab Alignment Students clear or alter default alignment positions using the Ruler bar. Ruler bar is a visual measuring scale displayed at the top of the workspace. Left-clicking on the ruler inserts custom alignment markers at precise coordinates. Dragging these custom markers left or right repositions the corresponding text dynamically. Decimal Tab Stops Word processors offer decimal tab stops to organize numbers neatly. This special marker aligns tabbed text so that numeric data sits around a fixed position. The software anchors figures automatically so that the decimal points match up vertically. Decimal tab stops are markers that align columns of numbers by their decimal points.

content.topicNotes: Arithmetic in Spreadsheets Entering Formulas Spreadsheet cells can contain formulae, which always start with an equals "=" sign. A formula is a mathematical expression that calculates new values from existing cell data. The equals sign instructs the spreadsheet to calculate the result instead of displaying raw text. Users typically use cell referencing when entering formulae. Using Cell References Formulae use cell references to link data dynamically across a spreadsheet model. A cell reference is the unique address of a cell formed by its column letter and row number. Typing "=A1+B1" adds the values inside those two specific boxes together automatically. The formula updates the calculated total instantly whenever a user modifies the underlying cell data. Arithmetic Operators Spreadsheets use specific arithmetic operators to perform basic calculations. Addition: the "+" sign. Subtraction: the "-" sign. Multiplication: the "*" symbol. Division: the "/" symbol. Indices (powers): the "^" symbol. To input percentages, use the "%" symbol. For example, "=60%" will appear as "0.6". Order of Operations Spreadsheets strictly follow the rules of BIDMAS to evaluate mathematical expressions. BIDMAS is an acronym that defines the correct sequence of operations: Brackets, Indices, Division, Multiplication, Addition, and Subtraction. Users must place brackets carefully to control which numbers add or multiply first.

content.topicNotes: Audience & Presenter Notes Audience Notes (Handouts) Audience notes are documents printed from a presentation software to distribute to the attendees. Handouts are structured layouts containing scaled-down versions of slides alongside blank lines for participants to write their own notes on. They help listeners follow along during a dense or highly detailed slideshow. Providing physical sheets allows the audience to review the technical data after the briefing has finished. Presenter Notes (Speaker Notes) Presenter notes are hidden reminders added to individual slides that only the person giving the talk can see. Speaker notes reference a dedicated text panel beneath the main slide workspace used to input key talking points. They assist the speaker by prompting them on complex figures and cues without cluttering the digital layout. Utilizing Presenter View displays these prompts on a private monitor while the audience looks at the clean slides on a secondary screen. Benefits of Notes Separating visible information from underlying data keeps the visual presentation highly professional. Presenters maintain better eye contact and pacing because they do not have to read text directly off the main projection screen. Handouts reduce the pressure on attendees to copy down every word during the live event. Both types of notes work together to ensure the content of presentations is communicated effectively.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Presentation

content.topicNotes: Analysing Audiences What is Audience Analysis? Audience analysis means identifying the characteristics of the people who will use or view a product. Audience analysis helps designers create content that is suitable and effective. Designers consider factors such as age, gender, interests, and technical ability. Understanding the audience ensures the product meets their needs and expectations. Purpose of the Product The purpose of a product influences the design choices a creator makes. An educational website for children uses different fonts and images than a business report. Designers match the tone, layout, and content to the intended purpose. Mismatching purpose and design can confuse or alienate the audience. Gathering Audience Information Designers collect information about their audience before creating a product. Questionnaires and surveys allow designers to gather opinions directly from users. A questionnaire is a set of written questions used to collect data from respondents. Interviews and focus groups provide more detailed feedback from potential users. Analysing existing products helps designers understand what the audience already expects.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Applying Information and Communication Technology > Using Software Applications

content.topicNotes: Analysing the Needs of an Audience Age and Technical Ability Designers adapt content based on the age group of the target audience. The target audience is the specific group of people a product is designed for. Younger audiences benefit from larger text, bright colours, and simple language. Adult audiences use smaller text, softer colours, and structured information like tables or charts. Technical ability describes how confident a user is with technology. A novice user needs simpler interfaces than an expert user. Accessibility Needs Accessibility means designing products so that all users can access and use them effectively. Designers consider users with visual impairments by using high-contrast colours and alt text. Alt text is a written description of an image used by screen readers. Audio content should include subtitles or transcripts for users with hearing difficulties. Considering accessibility ensures the product reaches the widest possible audience. Cultural and Language Considerations Designers consider the cultural background and language of their target audience. Using appropriate language ensures the content is clear and respectful. Symbols, colours, and images can carry different meanings in different cultures. Providing multiple language options increases a product's reach and usability.

content.topicNotes: Audio and Video Editing Audio Editing Software Audio editing software allows users to record, cut, and join sound clips. Users can add effects such as fade in, fade out, and noise reduction. Audio editing is used for podcasts, music production, and voiceovers. Video Editing Software Video editing software allows users to trim clips and arrange them on a timeline. Users can add transitions, titles, and background music. Video editing is used for films, school projects, and social media content. Key Editing Tasks Users can crop and resize media to focus on important parts. Users can adjust brightness, contrast, and colour balance for video. Users can export the final work into a suitable file format for sharing.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Software

content.topicNotes: Audio and Video Adding media You can add audio or video files to a web page using HTML tags. Use the <audio> tag to insert sound files. Use the <video> tag to insert video files. Media can make a website more interactive and engaging. Text placed inside the <video> container displays only if a user's browser cannot play the file format. Media controls Controls allow users to play, pause and adjust media. Add the controls attribute to display media buttons. Remove the controls attribute if users should not see playback options. Users can control media only when controls are available. Autoplay Autoplay starts media automatically when a web page loads. Add the autoplay attribute to enable automatic playback. Autoplay can annoy users or increase data usage. Designers should use autoplay carefully. Choosing media settings Web designers choose settings based on the audience's needs. Educational websites may display controls so users can replay content. Background music may hide controls if user interaction is unnecessary. Media settings affect the user experience.

content.topicNotes: Backing Storage vs Internal Memory Internal Memory Internal memory is used by the CPU during processing. It includes RAM and ROM. RAM stores data and programs currently in use. ROM stores start-up instructions. Backing Storage Backing storage stores data permanently. It is also called secondary storage. Examples include hard disk drives and solid state drives. Backing storage keeps data when power is off. Speed Difference Internal memory provides very fast access for the CPU. RAM allows quick reading and writing of data. Backing storage is much slower than internal memory. Computers load data from backing storage into RAM. Volatility Volatile memory loses data when power is turned off. RAM is volatile memory. Non-volatile memory keeps data without power. ROM and backing storage are non-volatile. Capacity and Cost Backing storage usually has a much larger capacity. It costs less per gigabyte than internal memory. Internal memory has smaller capacity but higher speed. Computers use both types to work effectively.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Storage

content.topicNotes: Bandwidth & Latency What is Bandwidth? Bandwidth is the amount of data that can be sent across a network in a set time. It is measured in bits per second (bps), megabits per second (Mbps), or gigabits per second (Gbps). Think of it like a pipe: a wider pipe carries more water at once. Higher bandwidth means more data can travel at the same time. What is Latency? Latency is the delay between sending data and its arrival at its destination. It is measured in milliseconds (ms). Low latency means less delay. High latency means a longer wait before data arrives. Bandwidth vs Latency Bandwidth and latency are different things. Bandwidth affects how much data travels at once. Latency affects how long it takes data to arrive. A network can have high bandwidth but still have high latency. Both factors affect how fast a network feels to a user. Impact on User Experience User experience in this context refers to how smooth and enjoyable it is to use a network service. Low bandwidth causes slow downloads and buffering when streaming video. High latency causes delays in online gaming, video calls, and web browsing. A good user experience needs both high bandwidth and low latency.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Factors Influencing Data Transfer

content.topicNotes: Barcode and QR Code Readers Barcode readers A barcode reader scans a barcode using a laser or LED light. A barcode is a series of vertical lines representing numeric data. Reflected light is converted into digital data by the reader. Supermarkets use barcode readers at checkouts. Barcodes allow fast and accurate product identification. QR code scanners A QR code scanner reads a square matrix code. QR stands for Quick Response. QR codes store more information than traditional barcodes. Smartphones scan QR codes using built-in cameras. QR codes link to websites, tickets or payment systems. Advantages and disadvantages of barcode readers Advantages of barcode readers Barcode readers provide very fast data entry at checkouts. Barcode readers reduce human typing errors. Disadvantages of barcode readers Damaged or dirty barcodes may not scan correctly. Specialised scanning equipment is required. Advantages and disadvantages of QR code scanners Advantages of QR code scanners QR codes store more data than barcodes. QR codes can be scanned using smartphones. Disadvantages of QR code scanners Poor lighting can affect scanning accuracy. Users may scan malicious QR codes that link to unsafe websites.

content.topicNotes: Benefits of Client-Server Networks What is a Client-Server Network? A client-server network links computers (clients) to a central computer (the server). Clients are the devices users work on. The server manages resources and services for all clients. This setup gives the network administrator central control. Control of User Access Rights The server controls who can access files and resources. Access rights are rules that say what each user can open, edit or run. An administrator can block or allow access for any user from one place. This keeps sensitive data safe. Centralised Administration All network settings are managed from the server. The administrator can update software or change settings for every client at once. This saves time compared to updating each computer separately. It also means changes take effect across the whole network quickly. Centralised Backup All user data is stored on the server. The administrator can back up every user's data from one place. A backup is a copy of data kept in case the original is lost. This reduces the risk of data being lost if a client computer fails. Shared Software and Storage Software is installed on the server and shared with all clients. This means only one licence may be needed instead of one per machine. Files are stored centrally, so any client can open the same file. Users can share and work on the same documents easily. Roaming Profiles and Hotdesking A roaming profile stores a user's settings and files on the server. The user can log in at any client computer and see their own desktop. This is called hotdesking - using any available workstation. It is useful in offices where staff do not have a fixed desk.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Benefits of Using LAN & Home Networks

content.topicNotes: Benefits of LAN What is a LAN? A LAN (local area network) connects devices in one building or site. For example, computers in a school or office. All devices on the LAN can share resources and communicate. LANs are managed by the organisation that owns them. Shared Peripherals A peripheral is a device connected to a computer, such as a printer or scanner. On a LAN, one peripheral can be shared by many users. This cuts costs because fewer devices need to be bought. For example, one printer can serve a whole office. Shared Data Files stored on a central server can be reached by all users on the LAN. A server is a computer that stores and manages shared resources. Users can open the same document from any device on the network. This keeps data in one place and makes backups easier. Flexible Access Users can log in from any device on the LAN. They see the same files and settings wherever they log in. This is useful in schools where students move between rooms. It also lets staff work from different desks. Media Streaming and Communication A LAN can stream audio and video files to any device on the network. Users can also send emails and instant messages across the LAN. This makes communication fast and cheap within the organisation. No internet connection is needed for these internal services. Shared Internet Access A LAN lets all connected devices share one internet connection. This is cheaper than giving each device its own connection. Network managers can control which sites users can visit. They can also monitor internet use across the whole network.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Benefits of Using LAN & Home Networks

content.topicNotes: Biometric Recognition What is Biometric Recognition? Biometric recognition identifies a person using unique physical or behavioural features. The system captures a sample and compares it to stored data. A match allows access to a system or building. Biometric data is usually stored securely in a database. Finger and Thumb Recognition Fingerprint recognition scans the unique patterns of ridges on a finger. Thumb recognition works in the same way using the thumb. The scanner converts the pattern into digital data. The system compares the data to a stored template. Face, Iris and Retina Facial recognition measures distances between key facial features. Iris recognition scans the coloured ring around the pupil. Retina recognition scans blood vessel patterns at the back of the eye. These patterns are unique to each individual. Hand and Voice Recognition Hand geometry recognition measures the shape and size of the hand. The system analyses finger length and joint positions. Voice recognition analyses tone and speech patterns. The system compares the sample to stored voice data. Advantages Biometric systems improve security because traits are difficult to copy. Users do not need to remember passwords or carry cards. The system provides quick access to authorised users. Each person has unique biological characteristics. Disadvantages Injuries, dirt or background noise can reduce accuracy. The system may produce false positives or false negatives. A false positive incorrectly accepts an unauthorised user. A false negative incorrectly rejects an authorised user. Storing biometric data raises privacy and security concerns.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Input & Output

content.topicNotes: Biometrics What are Biometrics? Biometrics use unique physical features to identify a person. A biometric is a measurable biological characteristic. Examples include fingerprints, facial recognition and iris scans. These features are difficult to copy or share. Types of Biometrics Fingerprint recognition scans patterns on a finger. Facial recognition analyses features of a face. Iris recognition scans the eye's unique pattern. Voice recognition identifies speech patterns. How Biometrics Protect Data Biometrics control access to systems and devices. Only authorised users can unlock the system. This reduces the risk of unauthorised access. It replaces or supports passwords. It may be used in smartphones or security systems. Data must be stored securely to prevent misuse. Encryption protects stored biometric information. Advantages Biometrics are convenient and quick to use. They cannot be forgotten or lost like traditional passwords. Unique biological traits make authentication very difficult to fake. Disadvantages Stolen biometric data cannot be changed or reset if compromised. Systems may fail to recognise users in certain conditions, such as injury or low light. Implementing and maintaining biometric equipment carries higher costs than standard password protection.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Potential Risks to Data & Personal Information

content.topicNotes: Blog, Forum, Wiki & Social Networking Blogs A blog acts as a personal online journal where an author publishes entries in reverse chronological order. Blog: short for 'weblog', a website containing personal reflections or hyperlinks to other sites. Owners update blogs regularly to share opinions or news with a global audience. Readers usually provide feedback by leaving comments at the bottom of each post. Forums An online forum provides a platform for people to hold asynchronous discussions through posted messages. Forum: an online discussion site where people can hold conversations in the form of posted messages. Administrators organise conversations into specific threads to keep different topics separate. Thread: a running commentary of messages linked to a specific original post. Wikis A wiki allows multiple users to collaborate by creating and editing web pages directly from their browser. Wiki: a website that allows collaborative editing of its content and structure by its users. It maintains a history of all changes, which allows editors to revert to previous versions if errors occur. Most wikis focus on sharing collective knowledge on specific subjects or projects. Social Networking Social networking sites enable individuals to build digital profiles and connect with friends, family, or colleagues. Social Networking: the use of dedicated websites to communicate with other users or groups. Users share multimedia content, such as photos and videos, and send private or public messages. These platforms use algorithms to suggest new connections based on mutual interests or existing friends.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Availability & Use of Online Information

content.topicNotes: Blu-ray Discs What is Blu-ray Blu-ray is an optical storage medium designed to store large amounts of data. Blu-ray uses a blue-violet laser to read and write data. A blue-violet laser has a shorter wavelength than a red laser. The shorter wavelength allows data to be stored more densely. Blu-ray discs are non-volatile storage devices. Storage capacity A single-layer Blu-ray disc typically stores 25 GB of data. A dual-layer Blu-ray disc can store about 50 GB of data. Blu-ray discs store much more data than CDs and DVDs. High-definition video requires large storage capacity. Blu-ray is suitable for high-quality media. Uses of Blu-ray Blu-ray discs are used to distribute high-definition films. Games consoles use Blu-ray discs for large games. Blu-ray discs store large software packages. Backup systems may use Blu-ray for archiving data. Blu-ray provides high-quality audio and video output. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Blu-ray discs offer very high storage capacity. Blu-ray supports high-definition video and audio. Disadvantages Blu-ray discs are more expensive than DVDs. Special Blu-ray drives are required.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Storage

content.topicNotes: Bluetooth What Bluetooth Is Bluetooth is a wireless technology that connects devices over short distances. It uses radio waves instead of cables. Bluetooth uses 79 different frequencies that are referred to as channels. The frequencies are distributed close to 2.45 GHz. Devices must pair before they can communicate. Pairing creates a secure connection between two devices. Common Uses of Bluetooth People use Bluetooth for wireless headphones and speakers. It also connects keyboards and mice to computers. Some phones share files using Bluetooth. Bluetooth works well for simple device-to-device connections. Advantages of Bluetooth Bluetooth removes the need for cables. It uses low power, so it saves battery. It is easy to set up for small devices. It works well in short-range environments. Disadvantages of Bluetooth Bluetooth only works over short distances. Has relatively low data transfer rates, making the transmission of large files noticeably slower. Interference from other devices can reduce performance. Bluetooth is not suitable for large networks.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Types of Digital Communications

content.topicNotes: Booking Trips and Events What are booking systems for Booking systems are used to reserve travel and event places electronically. Trips include flights, trains and holidays. Events include concerts, sports matches and theatre shows. Booking systems use databases to store availability. Users make bookings through websites or apps. Booking trips Airlines use booking systems to allocate seats on flights. Train companies use booking systems to reserve tickets. Travel websites combine transport and accommodation bookings. Payment is processed securely during booking. Selected seats or rooms are temporarily reserved in the database while transaction processing is completed. Confirmation details are sent electronically. Booking events Event organisers use booking systems to sell tickets. Seat numbers can be allocated automatically. Ticket availability is updated in real time. Electronic tickets can be sent by email. Entry can be verified using barcodes or QR codes. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Bookings can be made at any time. Double-booking is prevented automatically. Disadvantages System outages can stop bookings. Internet access is required to make bookings.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Online Goods and Services > Types of Services

content.topicNotes: Bookmarks and Hyperlinks Hyperlinks and anchors A hyperlink connects a user to another location or resource. An anchor uses the <a> tag to create clickable links. Hyperlinks can connect text or images. Hyperlinks improve navigation around websites. Bookmarks using IDs A bookmark links to a specific place on the same web page. A bookmark uses an id attribute to mark a location. The link can use <a href="#section1">. Bookmarks help users move quickly through long pages. Types of hyperlinks Internal links move users to pages within the same website. External links connect users to different websites. You can create email links using mailto:name@example.com. Links can open in the same window or a new window. Relative file paths A relative file path uses the current folder location. images/photo.jpg is an example of a relative path. Relative paths work when files move together between devices. Relative paths make websites easier to transfer. Absolute file paths An absolute file path gives the full location of a file. C:/Users/Documents/image.jpg is an example. Absolute paths should not link to local files in websites. Absolute paths may fail because other users have different folders.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Web Authoring

content.topicNotes: Breaks in Documents Page Breaks A page break forces content to start on a new page. Users insert page breaks instead of pressing Enter multiple times. Page breaks keep document layouts consistent. New chapters often begin after a page break. Section Breaks A section break divides a document into separate sections without pushing content to the next page. Users can apply different formatting to each section. Section breaks allow changes to margins, headers or orientation. A landscape table may require a section break. Column Breaks A column break moves content to the next column. Users insert column breaks in newsletters and brochures. Column breaks control where text starts in a column. They improve the organisation of multi-column documents. Choosing the Correct Break Users should choose the break that matches the required layout. Page breaks start a new page. Section breaks allow different formatting. Column breaks move content to the next column. Widows and Orphans A widow is a line of text left alone at the top of a page. An orphan is a line of text left alone at the bottom of a page. Users can adjust breaks to avoid widows and orphans. This improves the appearance and readability of a document.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Word Processing

content.topicNotes: Broadband, Mobile Broadband & Cellular Networks What is Broadband? Broadband is a high-speed internet connection that offers high bandwidth. Broadband supports many users at the same time. Broadband allows you to stream video, make video calls, and download large files. Broadband uses cables, such as copper phone lines or fibre-optic cables. Fibre-optic cables carry data as pulses of light, and are faster than copper cables. What is Mobile Broadband? Mobile broadband gives you internet access without a fixed cable. It uses a SIM card in a dongle, tablet, or mobile phone. A dongle is a small device you plug into a computer. You can use mobile broadband anywhere with network coverage. It is useful when travelling or in places without fixed broadband. What is a Cellular Network? A cellular network is a radio network used by mobile devices. It is divided into areas called cells. Each cell has a base station, a mast that sends and receives signals. When you move between cells, your device connects to the nearest base station. Mobile broadband runs over cellular networks. Generations of Cellular Networks Cellular networks are labelled by generation: 3G, 4G, and 5G. 3G was the first to support mobile internet browsing. 4G is faster and supports streaming video on the move. 5G is the newest generation. 5G offers very high speeds and very low delay (latency). Each new generation supports more data and more connected devices.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Factors Influencing Data Transfer

content.topicNotes: CAD and Graphics Editing Computer-Aided Design (CAD) Computer-Aided Design (CAD) software helps users create detailed technical drawings. CAD allows designers to model objects in 2D or 3D. CAD is used in engineering, architecture, and product design. Graphics Editing Software Graphics editing software allows users to create and modify images. Users can crop, resize, and add effects such as filters and text. Graphics editing is used for posters, logos, and digital artwork. Differences and Uses CAD focuses on accurate measurements and technical details. Graphics editing focuses on visual design and creative image changes. Both tools help users present ideas clearly and professionally.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Software

content.topicNotes: CAPTCHA Tests What is a CAPTCHA? A CAPTCHA is a test used to tell humans and bots apart. A bot is an automated program that acts like a user. CAPTCHA stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart. Websites use CAPTCHAs to block automated programs from misusing their services. Why Are CAPTCHAs Used? Bots can flood websites with fake accounts or spam. CAPTCHAs stop bots from submitting forms automatically. They protect online services such as login pages, ticket sites and comment sections. Only a real human should be able to pass the test. How CAPTCHAs Work A CAPTCHA sets a challenge that is easy for humans but hard for bots. A common type asks users to read and type distorted letters or numbers. The distortion makes it hard for a bot to read the text. Another type asks users to pick images that match a description, such as 'select all traffic lights'. reCAPTCHA reCAPTCHA is a widely used type of CAPTCHA developed by Google. An early version asked users to type words scanned from old books. This helped digitise printed text at the same time. A newer version simply asks the user to tick a box saying 'I am not a robot'. It checks mouse movements and behaviour to decide if the user is human. Limitations of CAPTCHAs Some CAPTCHAs are hard for people with visual impairments to complete. An audio version can be offered as an alternative. Advanced bots can sometimes solve simple CAPTCHAs using image recognition. Image recognition is software that identifies objects in pictures. CAPTCHA designers must keep updating tests to stay ahead of bots.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Potential Risks to Data & Personal Information

content.topicNotes: CD and DVD What are optical storage devices Optical storage devices store data using laser light. Data is stored as pits and lands on the disc surface. Pits and lands are microscopic changes that represent binary data. A laser reads the reflected light to retrieve data. Optical storage is non-volatile. Compact Disc (CD) A compact disc (CD) is an optical storage medium. A standard CD can store about 700 MB of data. CDs are used to store music, software and documents. Digital Versatile Disc (DVD) A digital versatile disc (DVD) is an optical storage medium. A DVD can store much more data than a CD. DVDs are commonly used for films and large software packages. Dual-layer DVDs increase storage capacity. DVD drives use a laser with a shorter wavelength than CDs. CD-ROM / DVD-ROM ROM stands for Read-Only Memory Data is pre-recorded at the factory. Ideal for mass-producing music, movies, or video games. Data cannot be altered or accidentally deleted. CD-R / DVD-R The letter "R" stands for recordable Data can be burned onto the blank disc once. Once written, it cannot be erased or overwritten. Good for making a permanent backup copy of a photo album. CD-RW / DVD-RW RW stands for rewritable Data can be written, erased, and rewritten multiple times. Ideal for moving files between computers but slower than a USB drive. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages CDs and DVDs are cheap to produce and distribute. Optical discs are portable and easy to store. Disadvantages Storage capacity is low compared to modern devices. Discs can be easily scratched or damaged.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Storage

content.topicNotes: Cameras and Camcorders Cameras and Camcorders A digital camera captures still images as digital data. A camcorder records moving video as digital data. Both store images or video on a memory card or internal storage. They can connect to a computer to transfer files. What is a Pixel? A pixel is the smallest dot of colour in a digital image. Every image is made up of thousands or millions of pixels. More pixels means the image holds more detail. Pixel stands for 'picture element'. Resolution Resolution is the number of pixels in an image. It is measured in megapixels (MP) for cameras. A higher resolution means a sharper, more detailed image. A lower resolution means less detail and a smaller file size. Frames Per Second Video is made up of many still images shown one after another. Each still image in a video is called a frame. Frames per second (fps) is the number of frames shown each second. More fps gives smoother video. Fewer fps makes video look choppy. Why Resolution and FPS Matter A high-resolution camera takes sharper photos. This is useful for printing large images. A camcorder with a high fps records smoother video. This is useful for sports or action footage. Higher resolution and fps both create larger file sizes.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Cell Referencing Relative Referencing Relative cell referencing happens when a cell address alters when you copy a formula to another cell. You write a relative reference using standard column letters and row numbers like "A1". Excel updates the row or column references to maintain the same relative distance from the original data. Absolute Referencing Absolute cell referencing refers to a fixed cell address that stays the same, no matter where you copy the formula. You create an absolute reference by placing dollar signs before the column letter and row number, like "$B$2". Excel keeps this exact cell locked to prevent errors when multiplying by constant values. Replicating Formulae Replicating formulae refers to the process of copying a formula across multiple cells using the fill handle. The fill handle is used to extend patterns, sequences, and formulas to adjacent cells. The fill handle is accessed by dragging the bottom-right corner of the selected cells. Excel changes the relative parts of the formula but keeps the absolute parts perfectly locked. You achieve accurate spreadsheet models by balancing both reference types during replication. Multiple Worksheets & Cross-Sheet Referencing What is a Worksheet? A worksheet is a single page inside a spreadsheet file. It contains a grid of rows and columns for storing data. A spreadsheet file can hold many worksheets at once. Each worksheet appears as a tab at the bottom of the screen. Using multiple worksheets keeps data organised and easy to find. Why Use Multiple Worksheets? Multiple worksheets let you separate data into clear sections. For example, a school might store each class's marks on a different worksheet. This avoids putting all data on one crowded page. It also makes the spreadsheet easier to read and manage. Working Across Worksheets You can link data between worksheets in the same file. This is called cross-sheet referencing. It means one worksheet can use data stored in another. Changes to the source worksheet update the linked cell automatically. This saves time and reduces errors from retyping data. Cross-Sheet Reference Format A cross-sheet reference names the worksheet and the cell. The format is: SheetName!CellReference. Example: Sheet2!B4 means cell B4 on the worksheet named Sheet2. You can use this reference inside a formula. Example: =Sheet2!B4+Sheet3!B4 adds values from two worksheets. Uses of Cross-Sheet Referencing A business might store each month's sales on a separate worksheet. A summary worksheet can then pull totals from each month's sheet. The summary updates when any monthly figure changes. This avoids copying data by hand and reduces mistakes.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Spreadsheet

content.topicNotes: Central Processing Unit (CPU) What the CPU Does The CPU is the main processor of a computer. CPU stands for Central Processing Unit. It processes data and instructions from programs. The CPU controls how the computer operates. Main Parts of the CPU The CPU contains the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU). The ALU performs calculations and logical comparisons. The CPU also contains the Control Unit (CU). The CU manages and coordinates CPU activities. The CPU is usually implemented on integrated circuit microprocessors, that often contain multiple CPUs Registers Registers are small, fast memory locations inside the CPU. They temporarily store data and instructions being used. Registers allow the CPU to work quickly. Examples include the accumulator and program counter. Clock Speed Clock speed measures how fast the CPU processes instructions. It is measured in hertz (Hz). A higher clock speed means more instructions per second. Faster clock speeds usually improve performance.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Processors

content.topicNotes: Cloud Computing What is Cloud Computing? Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet. Users access storage, software and processing power online. Data is stored on remote servers instead of local computers. A server is a computer that provides services to other computers. How Data is Stored and Managed Data is stored in large data centres owned by providers. The provider manages security, backups and maintenance. Users upload and download files through an internet connection. The system allows authorised users to share files easily. Types of Cloud A public cloud provides services over the internet to many users. A private cloud is used by one organisation only. A hybrid cloud combines public and private cloud features. Organisations choose the type based on security and cost needs. Advantages Users can access data from any device with internet access. The system reduces the need for expensive hardware. Providers handle updates and security management. Businesses can increase or decrease storage as needed. Disadvantages Users rely on a stable internet connection. Data breaches may occur if security is weak. Service outages can prevent access to important files. Storing data on remote servers may raise privacy concerns.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Online Goods and Services > Online Software

content.topicNotes: Chart Types Selecting Data for Charts Users must select the correct data before creating a chart. Contiguous data is stored in adjacent cells. Non-contiguous data is stored in separate cell ranges. Users can also select specified data ranges to include only relevant data. Bar Charts Bar charts use horizontal rectangular bars to represent values. Bar charts use horizontal bars to compare values between different categories. The length of each bar shows the value. Bar charts make it easy to identify the largest and smallest values. Column Charts Column charts display values using vertical rectangular bars. They compare discrete categories by displaying column height as the value. Vertical columns help highlight highs, lows, and trends across categories. Line Charts A line chart uses points connected by lines. Line charts show trends and changes over time. The horizontal axis often shows dates or time periods. Users can quickly identify increases, decreases and patterns. Pie Charts A pie chart is a circle divided into slices. Each slice represents a proportion of the whole. Larger slices represent larger percentages or values. Pie charts help users compare how parts contribute to a total. Scatter Charts A scatter chart displays data points using Cartesian coordinates to plot two numeric variables. It is used to show relationships and identify correlations between paired numeric values. It helps users see patterns, clusters, or outliers across numerical datasets. An example is plotting a person's height against their weight to check for correlation. Choosing the Correct Chart Users should choose a chart type that matches the data. Bar and Column charts compare categories. Line charts show trends over time. Pie charts show proportions of a whole. Scatter charts show relationships between two values. Chart title should be visible, meaningful, and located above the chart. Both X and Y axes should have clear labels with appropriate units of measurement.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Spreadsheet
ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Presentation

content.topicNotes: Classes & Divisions Purpose of <div> The <div> tag is used as a division element that groups content in a web page. A division element is a container used to organise related elements together. Developers use <div> to apply structure and layout to sections of a page. Classes for Styling A class is a reusable label used to apply the same style to multiple elements. A class allows consistent formatting across different parts of a web page. For example, a class called 'highlight' can style multiple paragraphs the same way. Reusable Formatting Reusable formatting means applying the same style rules to different elements using classes. This reduces repetition and keeps web pages consistent. Styles can be reused across headings, paragraphs, and divisions. Applying Styles to Divisions Styles can be applied to a <div> to control the appearance of grouped content. A styled division can change background colour, text size, or spacing. This helps make sections of a web page visually organised.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Web Authoring

content.topicNotes: Colour and Text Formatting Text Colour CSS uses the color property to change text colour. You can use colour names such as red or blue. You can also use hexadecimal or RGB colour values. Text colour can improve readability and appearance. Text Alignment CSS uses the text-align property to position text. You can align text to the left, right or centre. Alignment changes where text appears on the page. Correct alignment can make content easier to read. Font Weight Font weight controls how thick or bold text appears. CSS uses the font-weight property. bold makes text stand out from normal text. Bold text can draw attention to important information. Multiple Properties CSS can apply several formatting properties at the same time. You can combine colour, alignment, and font weight. Example: color: blue; text-align: centre; font-weight: bold;. Multiple properties help create a consistent design.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Web Authoring

content.topicNotes: Common Physical Risks Electrocution Hazards Spilling liquids near electrical equipment can cause electrocution, so drinks should not be allowed close by. Touching live cables with wet hands is dangerous. Damaged or frayed cables expose live wires, increasing risk, so the cables should be checked regularly by an electrician. Overloaded power strips can overheat and cause sparks. A residual current breaker (RCB) should be installed to prevent electrocution. Fire Hazards from Overloading Overloading sockets causes overheating and fires, so install sufficient wall outlets and limit extension leads. Faulty wiring or aging hardware can spark; perform routine safety checks. Keep flammable items like paper or curtains clear of heat sources. Ensure adequate room ventilation to prevent heat buildup. There should be a sufficient number of fire extinguishers. Never tackle electrical fires with water; use CO2 or dry powder units instead. Tripping Over Trailing Cables Loose cables across walkways are a major tripping hazard. Cable ducts should be used instead. Cluttered floors (e.g., bags, boxes) block safe movement and should be avoided. Poorly secured rugs or mats can slide. Falling Equipment Injuries Heavy equipment (e.g., monitors, servers) can fall if not secured. Unstable shelves or overloaded surfaces may collapse, so desks and shelves should be used that are strong and large enough. Protective barriers around high shelves decreases risk. Improperly stacked items can topple and should be avoided.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Implications of The Use of Digital Technologies

content.topicNotes: Common Malware Types Virus A virus is malware that copies itself and spreads. It attaches to files and activates when opened. It can corrupt or delete data. Users should scan downloads with antivirus tools before opening files. Trojan A trojan is malware disguised as legitimate software. It tricks users into installing harmful programs. It may create a backdoor for attackers. A backdoor is a hidden way to access a system. Only install software obtained from verified, official sources. Spyware Spyware secretly monitors user activity. It collects personal data without permission. It may record keystrokes or browsing habits. Run active anti-spyware software and avoid clicking suspicious links. Ransomware Ransomware locks files or systems. Attackers demand payment to restore access. It can spread through infected downloads. Maintain regular offline backups to restore files in case of attack. Worm A worm self-replicates and travels independently across computer networks. Worms operate without needing a host file or program to attach to. Worms propagate autonomously by taking advantage of flaws in network software security. Apply system updates and install firewalls to block network weaknesses. Adware Adware automatically displays unwanted pop-up advertisements on your screen. It is often bundled inside free software packages or untrusted downloads. It can slow down browsers and redirect search results to unsafe web pages. Use ad blockers and read installation options carefully to uncheck extra offers.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Potential Risks to Data & Personal Information

content.topicNotes: Communication Within Communities Target Audiences Each online community is aimed at a specific target audience. The target audience is the group of people the community is designed for. Social networks target a broad, general audience. Gaming communities target players of a particular game or genre. Professional networks target workers in a specific field. Example: LinkedIn targets business professionals. Communication and Collaboration Online communities let people communicate across the world instantly. Users can share ideas, files, and resources with each other. Teams can work together on projects without being in the same place. This is called remote collaboration. Video calls, shared documents, and group chats all support this. Global Scale The internet removes distance as a barrier to communication. A user in the UK can collaborate with someone in Japan in real time. Global communities spread knowledge and culture across borders. This has changed how people learn, work, and socialise.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Use of Online Communities

content.topicNotes: Compilers and Linkers Compiler A compiler translates high-level code into machine code so the CPU can run it. High-level code is a programming language designed to be readable by humans. Machine code is binary instructions that the computer understands. A compiler checks the whole program for errors before it creates an executable file. An executable file is a program file that the operating system can load and run. Linker A linker combines compiled code files into one complete program. Compiled code is code that a compiler has already translated into machine code. A linker adds library files so the program can use pre-written functions. A library is a collection of ready-made code that programmers can reuse. A linker creates a final executable file that the operating system can run. Why they are needed A compiler allows programmers to write in a language such as C and still run the program on a computer. A linker allows programmers to build large programs from smaller parts called modules. A module is a separate section of a program that performs one main task. A linker helps the program run by connecting references between different modules. Compilers and linkers reduce errors by creating a single working executable.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Software

content.topicNotes: Components of Network Systems What is a Network Component? A network is a group of devices linked together to share data and resources. Network components are the physical parts that make a network work. Some components are wired, using cables to connect devices. Others are wireless, sending data through radio signals. Cables A cable is a physical wire that carries data between devices. Cables give a fast and reliable connection. They are less affected by interference than wireless signals. Common types include Ethernet cables, used to connect computers to a router. Wireless Access Point and Booster A wireless access point (WAP) sends and receives radio signals. It lets devices connect to a network without a cable. A booster extends the range of a wireless signal. It repeats the signal so it reaches further across a building. Router A router directs data between networks. It sends data packets to the correct destination. Most home routers connect a local network to the internet. A router assigns each device an IP address. An IP address is a unique number that identifies a device on a network. Gateway A gateway connects two networks that use different protocols. A protocol is a set of rules for sending data. It acts as a translator between the two networks. For example, a gateway links a home network to the internet. Server A server is a computer that provides services to other devices on a network. These other devices are called clients. A file server stores and shares files. A web server hosts websites. Servers run continuously so clients can access them at any time.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Requirements for Connecting to a Network

content.topicNotes: Connecting to The Internet What is an ISP? An ISP (Internet Service Provider) is a company that connects you to the internet. Without an ISP, your device cannot access the internet. ISPs send data to and from your home through cables or wireless signals. Examples include BT, Sky, and Virgin Media. What is a Web Browser? A web browser is software that lets you view pages on the internet. It reads and displays web pages written in HTML. You type a web address, and the browser fetches the page for you. Common examples include Google Chrome, Firefox, and Safari. What is a Search Engine? A search engine is a website that helps you find information on the internet. It searches a huge index of web pages to find results. You type keywords, and it returns a list of matching pages. Common examples include Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo. What is Filter Software? Filter software blocks access to certain websites or content. It is used to stop users from seeing harmful or unsuitable material. Schools and parents often use filter software to protect young people. It can block sites by category, keyword, or web address.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Requirements for Connecting to a Network

content.topicNotes: Control, Measurement, Apps and Applets Control and Measurement Software Control software operates a system by responding to input from sensors. It sends instructions to actuators to perform actions. Sensors collect data from the environment. Actuators carry out actions. Measurement software collects, records and analyses data from sensors. Unlike control software, it does not operate or control the system. Uses of Control and Measurement Control software is used in: washing machines to control the drum and water pump traffic lights to change the lights at the correct time heating systems to switch the heating on or off based on temperature Measurement software is used to: record temperatures in weather stations monitor scientific experiments collect data in industrial processes Measurement software provides data, while control software uses data to make decisions and control a system. Apps and Applets An app is a small application designed for a specific task on a device. Apps commonly run on smartphones, tablets, and computers. An applet is a small program that runs within another application or a web page.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Software

content.topicNotes: Copyright Legislation Purpose of Copyright Copyright law protects the original work of creators from unauthorised use. Copyright: a legal right that grants the creator of an original work exclusive rights to its use and distribution. Legislation ensures that authors, musicians, and software developers receive credit and payment for their efforts. Modern laws prevent the illegal copying and distribution of digital media. Software Piracy Users must avoid software piracy to remain compliant with the law. Software Piracy: the illegal copying, distribution, or use of software without a valid licence. Companies use unique product keys to ensure that only legitimate buyers can activate the software. Breaking copyright law can result in heavy fines or even imprisonment for individuals and businesses. Legal Use and Licencing Individuals must obtain a licence before using copyrighted material in their own ICT projects. Licence: a legal agreement that outlines how a piece of software or content can be used. Single-user licence: grants permission to install and run the program on a single workstation. Site licence: allows an organisation, such as a school or business, to deploy the software across all devices located at one physical address.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Availability & Use of Online Information

content.topicNotes: Corporate House Style What is a Corporate House Style? A corporate house style is a set of design rules and brand guidelines defined by an organization. It ensures a consistent corporate image across documents, websites, and publications. It may include logos, colour schemes, font families and margins that make an organization immediately recognizable to the public. Purpose of a House Style A house style helps customers recognise the organisation. Consistent presentation improves brand identity.Brand identity is the visual image of a company. Features of a House Style A house style may define font styles and colours. It may include rules for logos and layouts.Layout is the arrangement of content on a page. These rules ensure all documents match. Uses of a House Style Organisations use house styles in letters and reports. They also use them in websites and presentations. Marketing materials often follow the same style. This creates consistency across all media. Advantages of Consistency Consistent documents are easier to recognise. Staff can create documents more quickly. A professional image builds customer trust. Consistency improves communication and presentation.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Applying Information and Communication Technology > Using Software Applications

content.topicNotes: Create and Label Charts Chart Labels A chart title explains what the chart shows. A legend identifies the data series using colours or patterns. Axis titles describe the data on each axis. Axis labels show the categories and values displayed on the chart. Data and Pie Chart Labels Data value labels display the exact values on a chart. Sector labels identify slices in a pie chart. Sector values show the numerical value of each slice. Percentages show each slice as a proportion of the whole. Formatting Values Users can format values to a specified number of decimal places. Decimal places are digits shown after the decimal point. Users can add currency symbols such as £ or €. Consistent formatting makes charts easier to understand. Adjusting Axis Scales Users can set the maximum and minimum values on an axis. An axis scale determines how values are displayed. Incremental values control the spacing between scale markings. Appropriate scales improve the readability of charts. Enhancing Appearance Users can extract a pie chart sector to emphasise important data. Extracting a sector separates it from the rest of the pie chart. Users can change colour schemes and fill patterns. Effective formatting makes charts more attractive and easier to interpret.

content.topicNotes: Image Cropping and Resizing Cropping Images Users crop an image to remove unwanted outer areas from the graphic. Cropping: the process of cutting away the edges of an image to improve framing or accentuate a subject. This process changes the dimensions of the image but does not scale the remaining content. Designers use cropping to remove background distractions and focus the viewer's attention on the most important part of the visual. Resizing and Proportions Users resize images by adjusting the number of pixels or the physical dimensions. Locking aspect ratio ensures height and width change proportionally so the image does not distort. Aspect Ratio: the proportional relationship between width and height. Changing only the height or width without locking the ratio results in a distorted image. Practical tasks often specify adjusting a single dimension without distortion (e.g., "resize the height to 3 cm while preserving aspect ratio"). Resampling Images Resampling changes the amount of image data when the physical dimensions are adjusted. Resampling: the process of increasing or decreasing the number of pixels in a digital image. Downsampling removes pixels to reduce file size, which is useful for web use or email. Downsampling: the process of reducing the pixel count of an image. Upsampling adds new pixels to increase the size, though this often causes the image to look blurry.

content.topicNotes: Data Entry Forms Purpose of Data Entry Forms Data entry forms provide a user-friendly interface that allows users to input data into a database table. Interface refers to a layout with visual elements designed for human interaction. Users type information into interactive input fields rather than editing database tables directly. Forms isolate the raw database tables from the end-user to keep data structure safe. Importance and Benefits Forms improve data integrity by reducing human input errors through validation checks. Data integrity means the accuracy, completeness, and consistency of data. Validation checks refer to automated rules that check if data is sensible. Interactive forms speed up data collection processes for businesses. Forms accommodate non-technical staff members who do not know how to interact with database tables. How and When Forms Are Used Database administrators deploy data entry forms when adding new client records or product details. Customers use online forms to input personal details during digital registration processes. Forms link directly to tables to update information in real time. Staff members utilise search parameters inside forms to find and update existing database records. Features of Well-Designed Forms Designers include clear labels next to every input text box to assist the user. Well-designed forms use drop-down menus and checkboxes to limit invalid user entries. Developers add navigation buttons to let users scroll through multiple records easily. Forms maintain a logical layout with appropriate spacing and visible text instructions.

content.topicNotes: Why Data Protection Legislation Exists Personal Data Protection Data protection laws ensure that personal information, such as names, addresses, and bank details, is kept secure. They prevent unauthorised access to sensitive data. Organisations must follow strict rules when handling personal information. Key Principles of Data Protection Data must be processed fairly, lawfully, and for specified reasons. Records must be accurate, relevant, adequate, and deleted when no longer needed. Firms must ensure robust security and respect data subject rights. Data cannot be transferred overseas without equivalent legal protection. Preventing Identity Theft Identity theft occurs when someone uses another person’s personal data without permission. Data protection laws help reduce the risk of identity theft by requiring organisations to protect user data. They also allow individuals to request corrections if their data is incorrect. Trust in Digital Services Users are more likely to trust a service if they know their data is protected. Data protection laws ensure organisations are transparent about how they use personal data. They also give users the right to know what data is being collected about them. Ethical Responsibility Organisations have an ethical duty to protect the data they collect from users. Data protection laws set standards for how data should be handled. They encourage organisations to be responsible with user information.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Implications of The Use of Digital Technologies
