content.topicNotes: Performing Searches Understanding Database Queries Database users perform searches by running a query. A query is a formal request to extract specific records from a database table based on criteria. Users define search conditions rather than looking through entire tables manually. Queries isolate the exact information required while hiding irrelevant records. How Queries Are Used Businesses use queries to extract targeted lists like outstanding customer invoices or low stock items. Search criteria act as filters to display records matching specific parameters. Criteria refer to the rules or conditions that data must meet to be selected. Users combine logical operators like AND, OR, and NOT to perform complex searches. Advantages of Using Queries Database queries save significant time compared to scrolling through large data sheets. Automated searches improve accuracy by eliminating human overview errors during inspection. Developers save query structures so users can run the exact same search instantly in the future. Databases dynamic links update query results automatically when underlying table data changes. Features of a Good Query Efficient queries target precise field attributes to minimise processing time. Well-designed criteria use clear comparisons like greater than or equal to operators. Good search queries output only relevant fields to make reports easy to read. Designers use wildcard characters to fetch records with incomplete search terms safely. A wildcard is a special character that represents one or more unknown text symbols.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Database Management

content.topicNotes: Desktop Computer What is a desktop computer A desktop computer is a non-portable computer designed to be used at a fixed location. A desktop computer usually consists of separate components such as a monitor, keyboard, mouse and system unit. The system unit contains the main internal hardware components. Desktop computers require a constant mains power supply. Desktop computers are commonly used in homes, schools and offices. Uses of desktop computers Desktop computers are used for office and business tasks such as word processing and spreadsheets. Schools use desktop computers for teaching and learning activities. Gaming and entertainment often use desktop computers due to high performance. Designers use desktop computers for graphics and video editing. Businesses use desktop computers for data processing and management. Desktop computers are typically connected to a network to share files, printers, and internet access. Advantages of desktop computers Desktop computers usually offer higher performance than portable computers. Internal components such as memory and storage can be easily upgraded. Larger cases provide better cooling for hardware. Desktop computers are often cheaper than laptops with similar specifications. Desktop computers are suitable for long periods of continuous use. Disadvantages of desktop computers Desktop computers are not portable and must remain in one place. A desktop computer requires more space than a laptop or tablet. Multiple cables are needed to connect external devices. A desktop computer cannot be used without a mains power supply. Desktop computers are unsuitable for users who need to work while travelling.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Drivers and Utilities Device Driver A device driver is system software that allows the operating system to communicate with hardware. The driver translates OS commands into instructions the hardware can understand. Examples include drivers for printers, graphics cards, and network adapters. System Utilities Utilities are system software tools that help maintain and optimise a computer. Examples include antivirus software, disk defragmenters, and backup tools. Utilities help keep the system secure, fast, and organised. How They Work Together The operating system uses drivers to control hardware devices. Utilities run alongside the operating system to improve performance and safety. Both drivers and utilities are essential for reliable computer use.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Software

content.topicNotes: Data and Information What is Data? Data is raw facts and figures that have no meaning on their own. Data has not been processed yet. Examples of data: 42, 07:30, or the letters 'XYZ'. These mean nothing without context. What is Information? Information is data that has been processed to give it meaning. Processing turns raw data into something useful. Example: '42' is data. 'The temperature is 42 degrees Celsius' is information. Context makes it meaningful. The Difference Between Data and Information Data is raw and unprocessed. Information is data that has been given context and meaning. Data becomes information after it is processed. Example: a list of numbers from a survey is data. The average score calculated from those numbers is information.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Applying Information and Communication Technology > Data & Information

content.topicNotes: Digital Cameras & Webcams Digital camera A digital camera is an input device that captures photographs and videos digitally. Images are stored as digital files on memory cards. Digital cameras use image sensors instead of film. Photos can be transferred directly to a computer. Many smartphones include built-in digital cameras. Advantages and Disadvantages of Digital cameras Advantages A digital camera captures real-world images quickly. Digital photos can be transferred and shared easily. Digital cameras allow for instant previewing, editing and deleting of images eliminating the cost and time of processing physical film. Disadvantages Image quality depends on resolution and lighting. Additional software may be required for editing. Webcams A webcam is an optical input device connected directly to a computer or built into a laptop frame. Its primary function is to feed or stream live video feeds in real time over the internet. Webcams facilitate video calling, virtual conferencing, and capturing simple still images or clips. Advantages and Disadvantages of Webcams Advantages Facilitates immediate face-to-face visual communication across remote geographical locations. Generally inexpensive to purchase when compared to high-end digital cameras. Compact and lightweight, often integrated into computer setups. Disadvantages Requires an active, ongoing connection to a host computer device to operate. Tends to offer lower image resolution and optical quality than dedicated cameras. Performance and stream smoothness rely heavily on the stability of the network connection.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Input & Output

content.topicNotes: Disadvantages for Organisations Security Issues Security issues arise when data stored on computer systems is at risk. Organisations store sensitive data such as customer details and financial records. If this data is lost or stolen, the organisation can face legal trouble and lose trust. Viruses and malware can also damage or destroy important files. Risk of Hacking Hacking means gaining unauthorised access to a computer system. A hacker breaks in without permission. Hackers can steal data, change records, or shut down services. An attack can cost an organisation money and damage its reputation. No system is completely safe from hacking. Greater Competition The internet makes it easy for new businesses to reach customers online. This means organisations face more competitors than before. A small business anywhere in the world can compete with large local firms. Organisations must keep improving to stay ahead of rivals.

content.topicNotes: Display and Print: Values and Formulae Values vs Formulae View Spreadsheets present calculated values by default within the cell workspace. Values view displays the final numerical or text result generated by a formula. Formulae view displays the actual functions and cells referenced instead of the results. This mode allows examiners and creators to verify the logical structure of the model. Spreadsheet Editing Tools Users can employ other editing utilities like copy, cut, and paste to replicate formulae efficiently. Copy duplicates selected data to the clipboard while leaving the original cell unaltered. Shortcuts like Ctrl + C for copy, Ctrl + X for cut, and Ctrl + V for paste expedite spreadsheet construction. Data Accuracy and Integrity Authors must maintain absolute accuracy during manual data entry and formula creation. Data accuracy refers to the process of ensuring that data is free from errors and correctly reflects real-world figures. A singular erroneous character can corrupt cascading cell dependencies and invalidate the whole data model. Cell dependency describes a relationship where a formula relies on the value of another cell to calculate properly.

content.topicNotes: Document Types Letters and Memos A letter is a formal written message sent to a person or organisation. Letters are used for job applications, complaints, and official communication. A memo (memorandum) is a short internal message sent within an organisation. Memos are used to inform staff about meetings or policy changes. Letters are sent externally; memos stay inside the organisation. Reports and Information Sheets A report presents findings or results in a structured format. Reports are used for business reviews, science write-ups, and investigations. An information sheet (also called a fact sheet) gives key facts on a topic. It is short, clear, and easy to read. Examples include a health fact sheet or a product information sheet. Newsletters, Posters, and Leaflets A newsletter shares news and updates with a group of readers. Used by schools, clubs, and businesses to keep people informed. A poster is a large, eye-catching document used to advertise or inform. Posters use bold text and images to grab attention. A leaflet is a folded or single sheet used to promote or inform. Leaflets are given out in shops or posted through doors. Choosing the Right Document Type Each document type suits a different purpose. Use a letter for formal, external communication. Use a memo for quick, internal messages. Use a newsletter to share regular updates with a group. Use a poster or leaflet to advertise an event or product. Use a report to present detailed findings. Use an information sheet to give clear facts on a topic. Standard Conventions Standard Conventions Standard conventions are features that follow agreed rules for a document type. A salutation is the greeting at the start of a letter (e.g. 'Dear Mr Smith'). A complimentary close ends the letter (e.g. 'Yours sincerely' or 'Yours faithfully'). The date shows when the document was written. The subject line states the topic of the document clearly. Logos and Why Conventions Matter A logo is a symbol or image that represents an organisation. Including a logo makes a document look professional and builds trust. Using standard conventions makes documents clear and easy to understand. They also make documents look professional and consistent. Following conventions helps the reader find key information quickly.

content.topicNotes: Education, News, Gaming & Auction Sites Education Sites Education sites provide learning resources over the internet. They offer videos, quizzes, notes and courses to help users study. Users can learn at their own pace, from any location. Seneca Learning is one example. News Sites News sites deliver up-to-date information about world events. Articles are updated quickly, often within minutes of an event. Users can read, watch or listen to news stories online. Examples include the BBC News website and The Guardian online. Gaming Sites Gaming sites let users play games through a web browser or app. Some games are single-player; others let many users play together online. This is called multiplayer gaming. Gaming sites may offer free games or charge a subscription fee. Auction Sites Auction sites let users buy and sell items online. Sellers list an item and set a starting price. Buyers place bids, and the highest bid wins the item. A well-known example is eBay. Some sites also offer a fixed 'buy it now' price.

content.topicNotes: Encryption What is Encryption? Encryption converts data into unreadable data called ciphertext. Unencrypted data begins as readable text called plaintext. An encryption algorithm scrambles plaintext into unreadable ciphertext. Only authorised users can read encrypted data. Decryption changes unreadable ciphertext back into readable form. Purpose of Encryption Encryption protects data from being accessed by attackers. It ensures privacy and confidentiality. It is used when storing and sending data. It builds trust in digital systems. It is essential for secure online services. Encryption on Hard Discs Hard disc encryption protects data that is stored locally on a computer. If the device is stolen, data remains secure, because only users with the correct key can access it. Encryption in Communication Emails can be encrypted to protect messages. Cloud storage uses encryption to secure files that are stored on servers. HTTPS websites use encryption for safe data transfer.

content.topicNotes: Enter, Organise & Refine Information Enter, Organise, Develop, Refine, Format Application software lets you work with information in five key ways. Enter: put data in. Organise: arrange it. Develop: add or extend content. Refine: improve accuracy. Format: control how it looks. Different types of software use these steps for different tasks. Word Processor A word processor lets you create and edit text documents. Enter: type text, insert images, graphs, and charts. Organise: use paragraphs, pagination, bullet points, tables, and text wrapping. Develop: add image captions, duplicate text and images. Refine: use spell check and a thesaurus. Format: change style, size, emphasis, and colour, then export or publish. Database Management Software Database management software stores and manages data in tables. Enter: type data into fields in a table. Organise: sort and filter records. Develop: add new fields and set relationships between tables. Refine: run queries, group records, and use validation. Validation checks that data entered is sensible. Format: produce reports, then export or publish. Graphics Software Graphics software lets you create and edit images. Enter: add images and text to a canvas. Organise: use layers and positioning. Layers let you stack elements so they can be edited separately. Develop: resize images and add animation. Refine: apply filters to improve or change an image. Format: choose export or publish options to save in different file types. Web Authoring Software Web authoring software lets you build web pages. Enter: add text, images, buttons, and animation. Organise: use tables and frames to lay out content. Develop: create hyperlinks and navigation between pages. Refine: add or edit menus. Format: apply font enhancements and alignment to improve appearance. Presentation Software Presentation software lets you build slide shows. Enter: add text, images, buttons, sound, and video. Organise: arrange content on each slide and set slide order. Develop: add animations and transitions between slides. Refine: add speaker notes and set timings for slides. Format: use a master slide to apply a consistent style, and change fonts. Spreadsheet Software Spreadsheet software lets you work with numbers and text in a grid. Enter: type numbers and text into cells. Organise: sort and filter data, use columns and rows. Develop: write formulae and functions, create graphs and charts. Refine: adjust chart features, use absolute referencing. Absolute referencing locks a cell address so it does not change when copied. Format: set cell, column, row, sheet, and print layout.

content.topicNotes: Evaluating and Improving Digital Products What Does Evaluating a Digital Product Mean? Evaluating means judging how well a digital product works. You check whether the product meets its purpose. You look at the ICT tools used and decide if they were the right choice. A good evaluation is honest and uses clear reasons. Identifying Strengths A strength is something the product does well. Ask: does it meet the needs of the user? Ask: is it easy to use and understand? Example: a leaflet that uses clear headings and a readable font is easy to follow. This is a strength in layout and design. Identifying Weaknesses A weakness is something the product does not do well. Ask: does anything make it harder to use or understand? Example: a spreadsheet with no labels on columns is hard to read. This is a weakness in organisation. Be specific — say exactly what is wrong and why. Evaluating ICT Tools and Facilities ICT tools are the software and features used to build the product. Examples: word processor, spreadsheet, image editor. Ask: was the right tool chosen for the task? Example: using a word processor to make a graph is a poor tool choice. A spreadsheet would be more suitable. Suggesting Improvements An improvement is a change that would make the product better. Link each improvement to a weakness you found. Example: 'The font is too small. Increasing it to size 12 would improve readability.' Good suggestions are specific and explain why the change helps. Making Modifications A modification means actually making the change to the product. Apply the improvements you suggested. After modifying, check the product again to see if it is better. This process of improving and checking can be repeated more than once.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Applying Information and Communication Technology > Reviewing Outcomes

content.topicNotes: Exporting Data from Databases Why Export Reports? Users export database reports to change or manipulate the data in other software packages. Exporting means transferring data from a database into a different file format for another application. Exporting allows analysts to create advanced graphs or charts in spreadsheet software. This process allows people to share critical database information without giving others direct database access. Hiding Data in Reports Database designers hide sensitive fields from reports to maintain data privacy and security. Data privacy means protecting personal information from unauthorised viewing or distribution. For example, a school clerk hides student home addresses on a class merits report shared with teachers. Hiding unnecessary data keeps the final report clean, relevant, and easy for the reader to understand. What are Labels? Labels display descriptive information used for identifying items or addressing mail. Users generate address labels to automate the distribution of letters to large groups of customers. Marketing teams print promotional labels directly from inventory data to advertise specific product details on packaging. Practical Tips for Exporting Data Export File Formats RTF (.rtf) exports formatted text for editing in word processors. CSV (.csv) exports raw comma-separated data for spreadsheet analysis. PDF (.pdf) exports a read-only layout view for shared reading. Text (.txt) exports basic plain text for broad software access. Hiding Search Criteria Fields Databases let you filter records using a field without showing it in results. Uncheck the Show box in design view to hide the field. Useful when a report title already explains the filter choice. Mail Merge and Address Labels Databases produce structured labels using filtered records. Labels are arranged in multi-column grids across pages. Each label contains embedded field tags (e.g., {First_Name} {Last_Name}) that populate automatically for every record. Labels often require student details printed in a specific position on every item.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Database Management

content.topicNotes: Exporting Files: Application Package Defining Exporting Users export files to save data in a format that other applications can recognise. Export: the process of converting a file from its native format into a different format for use in other software. This process allows for greater portability between different computer systems. Portability: the ability of software or data to be moved easily from one system environment to another. Spreadsheets and Databases Users often export data from Microsoft Excel or Access into plain text formats to transfer information. Microsoft Access: a database management system used to store, manipulate, and report on large sets of related data. CSV (Comma Separated Values): a file format where a comma separates each piece of data. Exporting an Access table as a CSV file allows an Excel user to open the data without needing the original database software. Word Processing Documents Microsoft Word users export documents to universal formats to ensure consistency across different platforms. RTF (Rich Text Format): a universal document format that retains basic formatting like bold and italic text. PDF (Portable Document Format): a file type that captures a document's layout so it looks the same on every device. These formats enable sharing with people who do not have Microsoft Office.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > File Management

content.topicNotes: Exporting Files: Generic File Format Need for Generic Formats Users require generic formats to ensure data can be opened across different platforms and software brands. Generic File Format: a standard file type that is not restricted to one specific application. These formats solve the problem of software incompatibility. Incompatibility: a situation where one software package cannot open or read a file created in another. Text File Formats Text-based generic formats allow for the transfer of data and documents between word processors and databases. .csv (Comma Separated Values): a plain text format that organises data into tables using commas. .txt (Plain Text): a format containing only characters with no styling or fonts. .rtf (Rich Text Format): a format that preserves basic styling like bold and italics. Generic Image Formats Standard image formats allow graphics to be viewed regardless of the operating system. .jpg: a compressed format ideal for digital photographs. .png: a format that supports transparency and high-quality detail. .gif: a format used for simple animations and low-colour images. .pdf: a fixed-layout format used to present documents and images exactly as designed. Audio and Video Formats Standardised media formats allow high-quality sound and moving images to be shared easily. .mp3: a generic audio format that uses compression to reduce file size while maintaining sound quality. .mp4: a generic video format used to store digital video and audio streams. These formats are compatible with almost all media players and mobile devices. Web File Formats Web browsers use specific generic formats to display content and apply visual styles uniformly. .html (HyperText Markup Language): the code used to define the structure and content of a web page. .css (Cascading Style Sheets): the code used to define the visual layout, colours, and fonts of a web page. These formats ensure websites look consistent on different devices. Compressed File Formats Compressed formats allow users to bundle multiple files into one smaller package for easier storage or emailing. .zip and .rar: common formats used to reduce total file size without losing any data. Compression: the process of reducing the size of a file to save disk space or speed up transmission.

content.topicNotes: Eye Problems and Headaches Eye problems Eye problems occur from prolonged use of computer screens. Staring at screens reduces blinking, which dries the eyes. Symptoms include sore, dry or irritated eyes. Blurred vision can occur after long periods of screen use. Eye strain is common when focusing on screens for too long. Causes of eye problems Poor screen brightness or contrast strains the eyes. Glare from windows or lights increases eye discomfort. Sitting too close to the screen increases eye strain. Long periods without breaks prevent eye muscles from relaxing. Small text forces the eyes to work harder. Headaches Headaches can be caused by prolonged screen use. Eye strain often leads to tension headaches. Poor posture can contribute to headaches. Stress from extended computer work increases headache risk. Dehydration during long sessions can worsen headaches. Prevention methods Regular breaks reduce eye strain and fatigue. The 20-20-20 rule helps relax the eyes. The rule involves looking 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes. Screen brightness and contrast should be adjusted. Anti-glare filters or screens can be fitted to minimise light reflections. Proper lighting and correct screen position reduce headaches.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Implications of The Use of Digital Technologies

content.topicNotes: Factors Influencing Data Transfer What is Data Transfer? Data transfer means moving data from one device to another. The speed of transfer is how fast data moves. It is measured in bits per second (bps). The volume of data is how much data is sent at once. It is measured in bytes (KB, MB, GB). Both speed and volume affect how well a network performs. Interference Interference is a signal that disrupts data transfer. It mainly affects wireless networks. Other wireless devices can cause interference. Examples: microwaves, cordless phones, nearby Wi-Fi networks. Interference slows transfer speeds. It can cause data to be lost or corrupted. Corrupted means the data arrives damaged and unusable. Blockages and Distance Blockages are physical objects that weaken a wireless signal. Examples: walls, floors, metal objects. The further a device is from the router, the weaker the signal. A weaker signal means slower transfer speeds. Wired connections are not affected by blockages or distance in the same way. Transfer Method: Wired vs Wireless The transfer method is how data travels across a network. Wired connections use cables, such as ethernet cables. Wireless connections use radio waves, such as Wi-Fi. The method chosen affects speed, reliability and convenience. Benefits and Drawbacks of Wired Connections Wired connections are generally faster than wireless. They give a stable, reliable signal. They are not affected by interference or blockages. However, cables limit how far a device can be from the network. Setting up cables can be costly and time-consuming. Benefits and Drawbacks of Wireless Connections Wireless connections let devices move around freely. They are easy to set up and add new devices. However, wireless signals can be slowed by interference. Walls and other blockages weaken the signal. Wireless is generally slower and less reliable than wired.

content.topicNotes: Features of Digital Devices Portability, Performance and Energy Consumption Portability means how easy a device is to carry and use on the move. A laptop is portable; a desktop is not. Performance depends on the processor and RAM. The processor (CPU) runs instructions; faster processors do more per second. RAM (Random Access Memory) holds data the device is currently using. Energy consumption is how much power a device uses. Portable devices need low energy use to preserve battery life. Storage and Expansion Capability Storage is where a device saves data permanently. Examples: internal hard drive (HDD), solid-state drive (SSD), or flash memory. Capacity is measured in gigabytes (GB) or terabytes (TB). Expansion capability means adding extra storage or features later. Examples: SD card slots, USB ports, or cloud storage. More expansion options make a device more flexible. User Interface A user interface (UI) is how a person interacts with a device. CLI (Command Line Interface): the user types text commands. Menu-driven interface: the user picks options from a list. GUI (Graphical User Interface): the user clicks icons and windows. Voice interface: the user speaks commands (e.g., a smart speaker). Gesture interface: the user uses hand or body movements (e.g., a touchscreen). Connectivity and Media Support Connectivity means the ways a device can link to other devices or networks. Examples: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, HDMI, and mobile data (4G/5G). More connectivity options let a device work with more equipment. Media support means the file types and formats a device can handle. Examples: MP3 audio, MP4 video, JPEG images, PDF documents. Good media support lets users play, view, and edit different content. Security Features Security features protect a device and its data from harm or theft. Software security protects data through programs and settings. Examples: passwords, PINs, fingerprint login, antivirus software, encryption. Physical security protects the hardware itself. Examples: cable locks, security cases, and biometric readers. Strong security reduces the risk of unauthorised access.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Features of Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Bitmap and Vector Graphics What is a Bitmap Graphic? A bitmap graphic is an image made up of tiny squares called pixels. A pixel is the smallest single point of colour in an image. Bitmaps are used for photographs and scanned documents. The more pixels an image has, the higher its quality. Bitmap Graphics: Enlarging and File Size If you enlarge a bitmap too much, the individual pixels become visible. This makes the image look blocky or blurry. This effect is called pixelation. Bitmaps with more pixels have larger file sizes. What is a Vector Graphic? A vector graphic is an image made up of coordinates, lines and shapes. These are stored as mathematical instructions, not pixels. Vector graphics do not pixelate when enlarged. They can be scaled to any size and still look sharp and clear. Vector graphics are used in video games, logos and technical illustrations. Bitmap vs Vector: Key Differences Bitmaps are made of pixels; vectors are made of coordinates and lines. Bitmaps pixelate when enlarged; vectors stay sharp at any size. Bitmaps suit photographs; vectors suit cartoons and technical drawings.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Graphics

content.topicNotes: Features of Online Communities What is an Online Community? An online community is a group of people who meet and interact over the internet. Members share interests, ideas or work together. Online communities can be social, educational or professional. They exist on websites, apps and platforms. Social Networking A social network is a website or app where users create profiles and connect with others. Users share posts, photos and videos with friends or followers. Examples include Facebook, Instagram and X (formerly Twitter). Social networks let people stay in contact across the world. Online Gaming Online gaming lets players take part in video games over the internet. Players can compete against or cooperate with others worldwide. Many games have built-in chat and friend lists. These features make gaming a type of online community. Examples include Fortnite and Minecraft. Online Workspaces An online workspace is a platform where people work together over the internet. Team members can share files, send messages and edit documents at the same time. Examples include Google Workspace and Microsoft Teams. Online workspaces help remote teams stay organised and connected. Virtual Learning Environments (VLEs) A virtual learning environment (VLE) is an online platform used for education. It is sometimes called a VLE for short. Teachers post lessons, tasks and resources for students to access. Students can submit work and communicate with teachers online. Examples include Google Classroom and Moodle. Wikis A wiki is a website where users can write and edit articles together. The content is created by the public, not one organisation. Anyone can add or update information on most wikis. Wikipedia is the most well-known example. Wikis rely on the community to keep content accurate and up to date.

content.topicNotes: Firewall What is a Firewall? A firewall is a security system that monitors network traffic. It checks data entering and leaving a network. It can be hardware or software. It helps protect systems from unauthorised access. Purpose of a Firewall A firewall blocks unwanted or harmful connections. It allows only trusted data to pass through. This reduces the risk of cyberattacks. It protects sensitive data on a network. How Firewalls Work Firewalls use rules to decide which traffic to allow. A rule is a condition that controls access. They inspect data packets before allowing entry. A packet is a small unit of data sent over a network. Types of Firewall Hardware firewalls are usually used to protect entire networks. Software firewalls are used to protect individual devices most of the time. Both types work together for better security. Users should enable firewalls on their devices.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Securing Data on Networks

content.topicNotes: Fixed and Portable Magnetic Hard Drives What is magnetic storage Magnetic storage stores data using magnetised areas on a disk. Data is stored as binary values. Binary values are represented using 0s and 1s. A read/write head accesses the data. Magnetic storage is non-volatile. Non-volatile means data is not lost when power is switched off. Fixed hard disk drive (HDD) A fixed hard disk drive is installed inside a computer. A fixed HDD is used as the main backing storage device. Data is stored on rotating metal platters coated with magnetic material. The disk spins at high speed during operation. A fixed HDD stores the operating system, software and user files. A fixed HDD offers large storage capacity at low cost per gigabyte. Portable hard disk drive A portable hard disk drive is an external storage device. A portable HDD connects to a computer using a USB cable. A portable HDD is used for backups and file transfer. A portable HDD can be moved between different computers. A portable HDD is also non-volatile storage. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of magnetic hard drives Magnetic hard drives provide large storage capacity at low cost. Magnetic hard drives are suitable for backing up large amounts of data. Disadvantages of magnetic hard drives Moving parts make hard drives vulnerable to physical damage. Access speed is slower than solid-state drives (SSDs). Portable hard drives can be lost or stolen more easily.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Storage

content.topicNotes: Fonts Font Face A font face is the design style of text. Examples include Arial and Times New Roman. Different font faces create different appearances. Users choose font faces to suit the document purpose. Serif and Sans-Serif Serif fonts have small decorative lines on letters and are commonly used in printed documents. Examples are Times New Roman or Georgia Sans-serif fonts do not have decorative lines and are often easier to read on screens. Examples are Arial, Helvetica or Calibri Point Size Point size controls the height of text. A point is a unit used to measure font size. Larger point sizes make text easier to read. Headings often use larger point sizes than body text. Font Colour Font colour changes the appearance of text and can highlight important information. Users should choose colours with good contrast for improved readability for users. Using Fonts Effectively Consistent fonts improve document presentation. Too many font styles can confuse readers. Fonts should match the purpose of the document. Clear fonts make information easier to understand.

content.topicNotes: Formulae and Functions in Spreadsheets Formulae vs Functions Formulae are user-defined mathematical equations used to perform calculations in a spreadsheet. A formula always begins with an equals sign and uses cell references, such as "=B1+B2+B3+B4". Functions are built-in, ready-made formulae that simplify complex calculations. A function uses a specific keyword followed by a range, such as =SUM(B1:B4). Cell ranges define a block of cells using a colon, which instructs the software to include all cells between the two references. Mathematical Operators Mathematical operators instruct the spreadsheet to perform basic arithmetic operations. The plus sign (+) executes addition, whilst the minus sign (-) performs subtraction. The asterisk (*) carries out multiplication, and the forward slash (/) handles division. The caret symbol (^) calculates exponents, which raises a number to a specific power. Numeric Functions "SUM" adds all the values in a specified range together. "AVERAGE" calculates the arithmetic mean by dividing the total sum by the number of values. "MAX" identifies the largest value, whilst "MIN" finds the smallest value in a dataset. "INT" rounds a number down to the nearest whole integer (=INT(8.9) returns 8). "ROUND" changes a value to a specified number of decimal places based on standard rounding rules (=ROUND(3.14159, 2) returns 3.14). Counting Functions "COUNT" registers cells containing numeric data, so =COUNT(A1:A5) returns 5 if all cells contain numbers. "COUNTA" evaluates all occupied cells, meaning that =COUNTA(A1:A5) counts text entries alongside numeric entries. An occupied cell is a cell that contains any form of data, including letters, symbols, or numbers. "COUNTIF" verifies entries against a rule, meaning that =COUNTIF(A1:A5, ">3") returns 2 if only two cells exceed the value of 3. Logical and Conditional Functions "IF" conducts a logical test and returns one value if the condition is true, and another if it is false (=IF(A1>5, "Pass", "Fail") outputs "Pass" if cell A1 contains at least 6). "SUMIF" accumulates data selectively based on a condition (=SUMIF(A1:A5, ">3") only adds values that are greater than 3). Nested functions embed one function inside another to allow the spreadsheet to evaluate multiple complex conditions.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Spreadsheet

content.topicNotes: Global Positioning System (GPS) What is GPS The Global Positioning System (GPS) is a satellite-based navigation system. GPS uses a network of satellites orbiting the Earth. A GPS receiver calculates its position using satellite signals. GPS provides location, speed and time information. GPS is widely used in smartphones and vehicles. How GPS works Satellites transmit signals containing time and position data. A GPS receiver picks up signals from multiple satellites. The receiver calculates distance based on signal travel time. At least four satellites are needed for accurate positioning. The process is called trilateration. Uses of GPS Drivers use GPS for route navigation. Delivery companies track vehicle locations. Smartphones use GPS for maps and location services. Aircraft and ships use GPS for navigation. Fitness trackers use GPS to record distance travelled. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages GPS provides accurate global positioning. GPS improves navigation and route planning. GPS operates worldwide, 24/7, in all weather conditions. Disadvantages GPS signals require a direct line-of-sight and can be blocked by tall buildings or tunnels. GPS accuracy can be reduced by poor signal reception.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Types of Digital Communications

content.topicNotes: Games Consoles What is a Games Console? A games console is a digital device built mainly for playing video games. It connects to a screen such as a TV or monitor. It uses a controller (a handheld input device) to take player commands. Examples include the PlayStation, Xbox and Nintendo Switch. Handheld Consoles A handheld console is a small, portable games console. It has a built-in screen, so no TV is needed. The Nintendo Switch and Nintendo 3DS are examples. Players can use them anywhere, making them very flexible. Avatars in Games An avatar is a digital character that represents the player in a game. Players often choose or design their own avatar. The avatar moves and acts based on the player's controller inputs. Avatars give players a personal identity inside the game world. Virtual Reality Games Virtual reality (VR) games place the player inside a simulated 3D world. Simulated means created by a computer, not real. Players wear a VR headset to see and hear the virtual world. Head and body movements control what the player sees. This creates a feeling of being inside the game. Multifunctionality Modern consoles do much more than play games. Multifunctionality means one device can do many different tasks. Consoles can stream films and TV shows. They can play music and browse the internet. Some let users video chat or download apps.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Graph Plotters What is a graph plotter A graph plotter is an output device used to produce large, precise drawings. It uses pens to draw lines on paper. Plotters are controlled by a computer. They are designed for high accuracy. Graph plotters are used for technical drawings. How graph plotters work A graph plotter is an output device that prints vector graphics. The computer sends instructions for the direction and length of each line. The plotter moves one or more pens over the paper. Pens draw continuous lines rather than dots. This produces very accurate output, making plotters suitable for technical drawings. Uses of graph plotters Engineers use graph plotters for technical diagrams. Architects use them for building plans. Designers produce large maps and charts. Graph plotters are used for computer-aided design (CAD). They are suitable for large-format printing. Advantages and disadvantages An advantage is extremely accurate line drawing. An advantage is high-quality output for large designs. A disadvantage is that graph plotters are slow. A disadvantage is that they are expensive. They are not suitable for general office printing.

content.topicNotes: Groups and Layers of Images Working with Layers Users place different parts of a graphic on separate layers to edit them independently. Layers: transparent sheets stacked on top of each other that hold individual parts of an image. Designers arrange the layers stack so the bottom layer acts as the background and the top layer appears at the front of the image. Use .png files for background transparency, as .jpg files do not support it. Grouping Objects Users group multiple elements together so they can move or resize them as a single unit. Grouping: the process of combining two or more objects so they behave as one item. This process preserves the relative position of objects within the group during layout changes. Users can ungroup the items at any time to modify an individual component again. Layer Visibility and Locking Editors allow users to hide specific layers to focus on a particular area of the document without distractions. Locking a layer prevents accidental changes to the content while working on other parts of the graphic. Locking: a function that restricts editing or movement of a specific layer or object. These tools help manage complex ICT projects that contain many overlapping shapes and text boxes.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Graphics

content.topicNotes: HTML Structure What HTML Is HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. HTML is used to create the structure and content of a web page. Web browsers read HTML to display web pages. HTML forms the content layer of a website. HTML Tags A tag is a code element that defines part of a web page. Tags are written inside angle brackets like . Tags identify elements such as headings, paragraphs, and images. Tags help organise content into a clear structure. Opening and Closing Tags Most HTML elements use an opening tag and a closing tag. An opening tag marks the start of an element: A closing tag contains a forward slash and marks the end of an element: The content appears between the opening and closing tags. Some HTML tags do not contain text and do not have a separate closing tag e.g. and DOCTYPE Declaration The DOCTYPE declaration appears at the top of an HTML document. It tells the browser which version of HTML the page uses. Browsers use the declaration to display pages correctly. The declaration helps ensure consistent behaviour. The HTML Element The element contains all the content of an HTML document. It is the root element of a web page. Most other HTML elements are placed inside the element like this: other elements The element defines the start and end of the web page structure.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Web Authoring

content.topicNotes: Head and Body Sections The Head Section The <head> section contains information about the web page. Information in the <head> section is usually not displayed on the page itself. The <head> section can contain page titles and links to stylesheets. Browsers use this information when loading the page. The Body Section The <body> section contains the content displayed in the browser window. Text, images, tables, and hyperlinks are placed in the <body> section. Users view and interact with the content in the <body> section. The <body> section forms the visible part of a web page. Page Titles Page titles are set using the <title> tag. A page title identifies a web page. The page title is stored in the head section. Browsers display the page title in the tab or title bar. Clear page titles help users identify and navigate websites. Head and Body Together The <head> section stores information about the page. The <body> section stores the content shown to users. Both sections are contained within the HTML document. Separating these sections improves organisation and maintenance. Website Structure Web developers use the <head> and <body> sections to structure web pages. A well-structured page is easier to create and maintain. Proper organisation improves consistency across a website. Good structure helps browsers display pages correctly.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Web Authoring

content.topicNotes: Headings and Subheadings in Word What Are Headings? A heading is a title that marks the start of a section in a document. Word processors like Microsoft Word have built-in heading styles. These are called Heading 1, Heading 2, Heading 3, and so on. Headings make a document easier to read. They break long text into clear sections. Readers can scan headings to find the part they need. Headings and Subheadings A main heading (Heading 1) marks a major section of the document. A subheading sits below a main heading. It gives more detail about that section. Heading 2 is used for subheadings. Heading 3 can be used for sections within a subheading. Automatic Table of Contents A table of contents (TOC) lists all the headings in a document. It shows the page number for each heading. Word can build a TOC for you automatically. This only works if you have used heading styles in your document.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Word Processing

content.topicNotes: Home Entertainment Systems What are Home Entertainment Systems? Home entertainment systems are digital devices used to watch, listen to, or record media at home. They include televisions, sound systems, personal video recorders, and disc players. Each device has a specific purpose within a home entertainment setup. Televisions and Screen Resolution A television displays video and audio content on a screen. Screen resolution is the number of pixels (tiny dots) that make up the picture. More pixels means a sharper, clearer image. Common resolutions: SD (640x480), HD (1280x720), Full HD (1920x1080), 4K (3840x2160), and 8K (7680x4320). Higher resolution screens show more detail but cost more. Smart TVs A smart TV is a television with built-in internet connection. It lets users stream content from services like Netflix or BBC iPlayer. Users can browse the web and use apps directly on the TV. Smart TVs do not need a separate streaming device. Sound Systems A sound system improves the audio quality beyond built-in TV speakers. Examples include soundbars and surround sound setups. Sound systems are usually connected via USB or wirelessly via Bluetooth. Blu-ray, DVD Players, and PVR A DVD player reads DVDs to play films and video content. DVDs usually store video at 480p (SD) quality. A Blu-ray player reads Blu-ray discs. Blu-ray supports HD and 4K video quality. Blu-ray gives a sharper picture and better sound than DVD. Personal Video Recorders (PVR) are devices that record live TV content in a hard disk storage to watch later.

content.topicNotes: IP Address What an IP Address Is An IP address identifies a device on a network. IP stands for Internet Protocol. Networks use IP addresses to send data to the correct device. Each device on a network needs an IP address. How IP Addresses Work A device uses its IP address to send and receive data. Routers read IP addresses to forward data between networks. A router is a device that directs data between networks. This process allows access to the internet. Types of IP Address IPv4 uses four numbers separated by dots like this: 203.0.113.195 IPv6 uses longer addresses to provide more unique values like this:2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7344 IPv4 means Internet Protocol version 4. IPv6 means Internet Protocol version 6.

content.topicNotes: Images in Web Pages Inserting Images The tag inserts an image into a web page. Images improve the appearance and understanding of content. The image source identifies the image file location. Web developers should use relevant images. Alternative Text Alternative text is stored in the alt attribute like ![image](cat.jpg) Alt text describes an image if it cannot load. Screen readers use alt text to help visually impaired users. Alt text improves accessibility. Image Paths A relative path uses a file location within the website folder like ![image](images/cat.png) An absolute path uses the full web address of a file like ![image](https://example.com/images/dog.png) Relative paths make websites easier to move. Absolute paths often point to external resources. Image Formats JPEG files store photographs with small file sizes. PNG files support transparency and high image quality. GIF files support simple animations. Different image formats suit different purposes. Size and Aspect Ratio Web developers can change image width and height like width="500" Aspect ratio is the relationship between image width and height. Keeping the aspect ratio prevents image distortion. Correct sizing improves page appearance.

content.topicNotes: Impact on Employment How Technology Changes Employment Technology changes the way people work. Some jobs disappear, but new ones appear. The skills workers need also change. These changes affect many industries, from farming to banking. New Job Opportunities New technology creates jobs that did not exist before. Examples include app developers, data analysts, and cybersecurity experts. These roles grew because of computers and the internet. Businesses also need people to manage and maintain new systems. Changing Nature of Jobs Technology changes what workers do in their existing jobs. A shop worker may now use a barcode scanner and computerised till. A doctor may use software to store and check patient records. The core role stays the same, but the day-to-day tasks change. New Skills Requirements Workers must learn new skills to keep up with technology. Digital skills (the ability to use computers and software) are now needed in most jobs. Employers expect staff to use tools like spreadsheets and email. Workers who lack these skills may struggle to find or keep work. Potential Job Loss Automation (using machines or software to do tasks) can replace human workers. Factory robots now do jobs once done by people on assembly lines. Self-checkout machines have reduced the need for checkout staff. This is called technological unemployment. It means job loss caused by technology replacing workers. Balancing the Impact Technology removes some jobs but creates others. Retraining (learning new skills for a different role) helps workers adapt. Governments and employers can offer training programmes. The overall effect on employment depends on how quickly workers can learn new skills.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Impact of The Internet on Individuals

content.topicNotes: Impact on Lifestyle and Behaviour Shopping and Retail People can buy goods online at any time, from anywhere. This reduces the need to visit physical shops. Fewer high-street shoppers can lead to shop closures. Price comparison sites let buyers find the cheapest deals quickly. Online shopping has changed spending habits and consumer behaviour. Banking and Finance Online banking lets people check accounts and transfer money via a website or app. Customers no longer need to visit a bank branch for most tasks. This has led to many bank branches closing. People can pay bills and manage finances at any hour of the day. Entertainment and Leisure Streaming services let people watch films, TV and listen to music on demand. Examples include Netflix, BBC iPlayer and Spotify. People watch less scheduled television as a result. Gaming online connects players around the world at any time. Leisure habits have shifted from physical to digital activities. Communication and Social Life Social media and messaging apps let people communicate instantly. People stay in contact with friends and family across the world. Face-to-face meetings happen less often for some people. Online communities form around shared interests. This can affect social skills and real-world relationships. Work and Education Remote working lets employees work from home using the internet. Online learning platforms provide courses and resources at any time. People can retrain or study without attending a physical location. Flexible working patterns have changed daily routines for many. This can improve work-life balance but may blur home and work boundaries. Health and Wellbeing Online health services let people book appointments or get advice without visiting a clinic. Health apps help people track fitness, diet and sleep. However, too much screen time can harm sleep and mental health. Reduced physical activity from online services can affect fitness levels. Access to online information helps people make informed health choices.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Online Goods and Services > Impact of Online Services

content.topicNotes: Impact on Services, Learning & Leisure Better Access to Information The internet gives people quick access to vast amounts of information. Search engines let users find answers in seconds. Online encyclopaedias and news sites are available at any time. This is far faster than using printed books or visiting a library. Better Access to Services Many services are now available online, 24 hours a day. Online banking lets people check accounts and pay bills at home. Shopping online means people can buy goods without visiting a shop. New Ways of Learning Technology has created new ways to learn outside the classroom. E-learning means studying using digital tools and the internet. Examples include video lessons, online quizzes, and virtual classrooms. Students can learn at their own pace and revisit topics easily. Distance learning lets people study from home, anywhere in the world. Entertainment and Leisure Opportunities Technology has widened the range of entertainment choices. Streaming services let users watch films and TV on demand. Music can be played instantly using apps and online platforms. Online gaming lets people play with others around the world. Social media lets people share photos, videos, and messages. Impact on Daily Life Digital technology has changed how people spend their time. People can work, learn, and relax using the same device. Access to services and entertainment is faster and more convenient. However, not everyone has equal access to these benefits.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Impact of The Internet on Individuals

content.topicNotes: Impact on Working Practices How Technology Changes Work Technology has changed the way people work. Workers can now connect to colleagues and systems from almost anywhere. This has led to two key changes: collaborative working and flexible working. Collaborative working means people work together, often remotely. Flexible working means people choose when and where they work. Collaborative Working Collaborative working lets people work on the same task at the same time. They do not need to be in the same room. Tools like shared documents, video calls and cloud storage make this possible. Cloud storage keeps files online so anyone can access them. Example: a team edits a shared spreadsheet from different locations. Benefits of Collaborative Working Teams can share ideas and files instantly. Work can continue even when people are in different time zones. Fewer physical meetings are needed. This saves time and travel costs. Version control tools show who changed what in a shared document. Flexible Working Flexible working means staff can choose their hours or work location. Working from home (remote working) is one common form. Remote working uses a broadband connection and a laptop or PC. Flexitime lets workers pick their start and finish times. Hot-desking means workers share desks rather than having their own. Benefits of Flexible Working Workers can fit work around family or personal needs. Employers can hire people from a wider area. Less time is spent commuting. Commuting means travelling to and from a workplace. Office costs can fall because fewer desks are needed. Drawbacks of Flexible and Collaborative Working Working from home can feel isolating. It can be harder to manage a team you cannot see in person. Sharing files online raises security risks. Sensitive data could be seen by the wrong people. A reliable internet connection is needed at all times.

content.topicNotes: The Information Gap What is the Information Gap? Some people have easy access to information. Others do not. This difference is called the gap between information rich and information poor. Information rich: people who can find, access and use information easily. Information poor: people who struggle to access or use information. Being Information Rich Information rich people have good access to information sources. They may have a computer, a smartphone or fast internet at home. They can search for news, facts and help whenever they need it. This gives them an advantage in education and work. Being Information Poor Information poor people have limited access to information. They may lack a device, an internet connection, or the skills to search online. This can make it harder to learn, find jobs or access public services. The gap can exist within a country, not just between countries. Causes of the Gap Cost: devices and internet plans can be too expensive for some people. Location: rural areas may have slow or no broadband. Skills: some people have not been taught how to use digital tools. Language: most online content is in a small number of languages. Effects of the Gap Information poor people may miss out on job adverts or training. They may not find health or safety information when they need it. The gap can make existing inequalities worse over time. Governments and charities work to close the gap through free Wi-Fi and digital skills training.

content.topicNotes: Information Reliability Evaluating Content Accuracy Users must evaluate the accuracy of digital information because anyone can publish content on the Internet. You should cross-reference facts with other trusted sources to ensure the data remains consistent. Cross-referencing: the process of checking a piece of information against several different sources. Reliable websites often cite their references and provide evidence for the claims they make. Author Credentials and Bias Students should check the credentials of the author to determine if they possess expertise in the subject. Credentials: the qualifications, experience, or education that prove a person is an expert. You must identify potential bias where an author might present a one-sided view to influence the reader. Bias: a prejudice in favour of or against one thing, person, or group in a way considered to be unfair. Material may be unreliable if the publisher intentionally distributes false details or fails to revise facts. Currency of Information You must check the publication or 'last updated' date to ensure the information is current and not obsolete. Currency: the quality of being up-to-date and relevant to the present time. Outdated information can lead to incorrect conclusions, especially in fast-moving fields like technology or science. Reliable websites regularly maintain their content to reflect the most recent developments or findings. Website Purpose and URL You should examine the top-level domain of a URL to understand the primary purpose of a website. Top-level domain: the final part of a domain name, such as .gov for government or .edu for education. Websites with .gov or .ac.uk suffixes generally provide more reliable and objective data than personal blogs. You must determine if a site intends to inform, persuade, or sell a product to judge its objectivity.

content.topicNotes: Input & Output Devices Input Devices Input devices allow users to enter data into a computer system. They send data and instructions to the CPU. Examples include keyboards, mice, microphones, numeric keypads, touchpads, digital cameras and scanners. Input devices help users control computer operations. Output Devices Output devices present information from the computer to the user. They display or produce the results of processing. Examples include monitors, printers, speakers, and projectors. Output devices make processed data understandable.

content.topicNotes: Integrating Objects in a Document Images and Callouts/Autoshapes An image is a picture or photograph added to a document. A callout is a shape with a text bubble, used to label or explain something. Autoshapes are ready-made shapes such as arrows, stars, or banners. These objects make documents clearer and more visual. Grouping Objects Grouping means joining two or more objects so they act as one. You can move, resize, or format the group all at once. This is useful when a chart and its label must stay together. To ungroup, you split the objects apart again. Layering Objects Layering controls which object appears in front of or behind another. Each object sits on its own layer, like sheets of paper stacked up. 'Bring to front' moves an object on top of others. 'Send to back' moves it behind others. Layering lets you overlap images, shapes, and text boxes neatly.

content.topicNotes: Internal Memory: ROM & RAM What Is Internal Memory Internal memory stores data and instructions used by the CPU. It is located inside the computer system. Internal memory allows fast access to data. The two main types are ROM and RAM. Read Only Memory (ROM) ROM stands for Read Only Memory. ROM stores essential instructions needed to start the computer. Data in ROM does not change during normal use. ROM keeps its contents when the power is turned off. ROM is used for software that usually does not change. This is also called firmware. An important example are boot-up instructions, often called BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) that decide what to do when the computer starts. Random Access Memory (RAM) RAM stands for Random Access Memory. RAM stores programs and data currently in use. RAM allows fast read and write access. RAM loses its contents when the power is turned off. Comparing ROM and RAM ROM is non-volatile, which means it keeps data without power. RAM is volatile, which means it needs power to store data. ROM stores start-up instructions. RAM stores working data and running programs. Why Internal Memory Matters Internal memory affects how quickly a computer runs programs. More RAM allows more programs to run at the same time. ROM ensures the computer starts correctly every time. Both types of memory support normal computer operation.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Memory

content.topicNotes: Internet & Emails Safe Internet Use Only visit websites recommended by teachers or trusted sources. Use search engines that filter content to ensure age-appropriate results. Avoid clicking on unknown links or pop-ups that may contain malware. Email Safety Never open or reply to emails from unknown senders. Be cautious of phishing emails that ask for personal or financial information. Always verify the sender’s email address before responding. Risks of Sharing Personal Data via Email Sending personal information like your address or phone number via email can lead to identity theft. Avoid sharing passwords or bank details over email. Use secure methods, such as encrypted email services, when necessary.
