content.topicNotes: Internet Banking What is internet banking Internet banking is a system that allows customers to manage bank accounts online. Customers access services using a web browser or mobile app. Secure login details are required. Internet banking uses computer networks to process transactions. Banking services are available without visiting a bank branch. Services provided by internet banking Account balances can be viewed online. Money can be transferred between accounts. Bills can be paid electronically. Statements can be downloaded digitally. Standing orders and direct debits can be managed. Security features Usernames and passwords protect account access. Two-factor authentication adds extra security. Two-factor authentication requires a second verification step. Encryption protects data during transmission. Automatic logout reduces the risk of unauthorised access. Advantages and Disadvantages for Customers Advantages Banking services are available 24 hours a day. Transactions can be completed quickly and conveniently. Disadvantages Internet access is required. Security risks exist if users do not follow safe practices. Advantages and Disadvantages for Banks Advantages Decreased running expenses due to fewer physical premises and lower staffing requirements. Ability to serve a wider customer base without geographical limits. Disadvantages Greater exposure to online threats and cybercrime. Substantial investment needed to establish and maintain robust IT security software.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Online Goods and Services > Types of Services

content.topicNotes: Internet Shopping What is Internet Shopping? Internet shopping allows customers to buy goods online using a website. The system stores product details in an online database. Online Payment Process The customer adds items to an online shopping basket and proceeds to checkout. The website collects delivery details and payment information through a secure web page. The system encrypts the payment data, which means it converts the data into a coded form to keep it safe. The payment gateway sends the transaction request to the customer’s bank for authorisation. The bank approves or declines the payment and sends a confirmation message back to the online shop. Advantages Customers can shop at any time of day without visiting a physical store. Customers can compare prices quickly between different websites. Retailers can reach a global market instead of only local customers. Online shops reduce costs because they do not need as many physical premises. Customers can read reviews from other buyers before making a purchase. Disadvantages Customers cannot physically examine or try products before buying them. Customers may experience delivery delays or additional shipping costs. Online shops face security risks such as hacking and fraud. Customers must provide personal and financial data, which could be stolen if security is weak. Some customers may struggle if they have limited internet access or low digital skills.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Online Goods and Services > Types of Services

content.topicNotes: Introduction to Data Models What is a Data Model? A data model is a mathematical or logical representation of a real-world situation created inside a spreadsheet. A spreadsheet model is a system that allows users to mock up scenarios and predict outcomes. Users input variables to see how changes affect the overall results. A variable is a value or piece of data that can change depending on the situation. Data types, Number and Text Data types define the nature of values stored in a spreadsheet cell. Numbers represent raw numerical values used in formulas and automated calculations. Text or labels act as descriptive headers and qualitative categories for data. Selecting correct types ensures formulas run accurately and prevents errors. Spreadsheet Structure Gridlines divide a spreadsheet into rows and columns. Rows run horizontally across the screen and are identified by numbers. Columns run vertically down the screen and are identified by letters. Intersections of rows and columns form individual boxes called cells. Each cell has a unique cell reference to identify its location. A cell reference is a combination of the column letter and row number, such as A1. Uses of Spreadsheet Models Businesses use spreadsheet models to create financial reports and manage bookkeeping. Organisations project future profits by testing different financial figures. Event planners forecast total costs by changing the estimated number of guests. Scientists model environmental data to track changes over time.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Spreadsheet

content.topicNotes: Database Structure What Are Databases? A database is an organised collection of data stored electronically. A file represents a single complete collection of structured data. A record represents a single complete set of data about one specific item or person. A record forms a complete row in a database table. A field represents a single category of data within a record. A field forms a single column in a database table. Flat-file Databases A flat-file database stores all data in a single table consisting of rows and columns. Users find flat-file databases easy to set up and understand for simple data storage. Flat-file structures cause significant data redundancy because users must repeat the same information across multiple rows. Data redundancy is the unnecessary duplication of data within a database. Relational Databases A relational database stores data across multiple linked tables. A primary key is a field that uniquely identifies each record in a table. A foreign key is a primary key from one table that appears in another table to link them together. Relational structures reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity. Data integrity is the accuracy and consistency of data stored in a database. Database Relationships In relational databases, primary and foreign keys link different tables together. One-to-many is the most frequent relationship type. One row in a main table matches several rows in a linked table. For example, one client can make many purchases, but each purchase links to one client. Database Comparison Relational databases prevent data inconsistency when users update records because the data resides in only one place. Data inconsistency occurs when different versions of the same data exist in a system. Relational databases require more complex design skills and higher processing power than flat-file databases. Flat-file databases operate much faster when users handle very small amounts of information. Data Types Database designers assign a specific data type to each field to ensure validation. Alphanumeric fields accept text, numbers, symbols, and spaces. Numeric fields store numbers that computers can use in mathematical calculations. Numeric subtypes include integer for whole numbers and decimal for fractional numbers. Boolean fields store only two possible values, such as Yes or No. Date fields store calendar dates and times in a standardised format.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Database Management

content.topicNotes: Introduction to Presentations What is a Presentation? A presentation is a structured collection of slides used to deliver information to an audience. Slide: A single screen or page within a presentation. Presenters use multimedia elements to make the information engaging. Multimedia: The combination of different content forms such as text, images, audio, and video. Uses of Presentations Teachers deliver educational lessons in classrooms to explain complex topics. Managers pitch new business ideas or financial updates to corporate investors. Individuals share information or promote awareness at public community meetings. Audience and Purpose Creators must design slides to meet the specific needs of the target audience. Target audience: The specific group of people for whom the presentation is intended. Presenters use short, simple words and bright, colourful layouts for young children. Professionals use formal language, charts, and minimal decoration for business executives. Consistency and Colour Designers apply a consistent layout across all slides to make the presentation look organised. Clear colour schemes ensure that the text is easily readable against the background. Colour scheme: A planned combination of colours chosen to give a unified appearance. Consistent placement of titles and navigation buttons helps the audience follow the structure.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Presentation

content.topicNotes: Keyboard and Numeric Keypad Keyboard as an input device A keyboard is an input device used to enter text, numbers and commands. Users press keys to input data into the computer. A standard keyboard includes alphabetic keys, number keys and function keys. Function keys perform specific actions depending on the software. Keyboards are commonly used with desktop and laptop computers. Uses of a keyboard Keyboards are used for typing letters, reports and emails. Programmers use keyboards to write and edit code. Data entry operators use keyboards to input large amounts of text. Keyboard shortcuts improve efficiency. Keyboards allow precise and controlled text input. Numeric keypad A numeric keypad is a set of number keys arranged like a calculator. A numeric keypad is usually located on the right side of a full-size keyboard. Standalone numeric keypads can be connected separately. Numeric keypads are used in ATMs, point-of-sale terminals and calculators. The layout improves speed and accuracy when entering numbers. Advantages and disadvantages of a keyboard Advantages of a keyboard A keyboard allows accurate entry of text and commands. A keyboard is suitable for long documents and detailed input. Disadvantages of a keyboard Typing can be slow for inexperienced users. Prolonged use may cause repetitive strain injury (RSI), although this can be reduced by using ergonomic keyboards. Advantages and disadvantages of a numeric keypad Advantages of a numeric keypad A numeric keypad speeds up entry of numerical data. The calculator-style layout reduces input errors. Disadvantages of a numeric keypad A numeric keypad is mainly suitable for numbers only. A numeric keypad adds extra space to the keyboard.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Input & Output

content.topicNotes: Laptop Computer What is a laptop computer A laptop computer is a portable computer designed for use in different locations. It integrates the screen, keyboard, touchpad and system unit into one device. A touchpad is a flat surface used to control the on-screen pointer. Laptops can operate using a rechargeable battery. They are lightweight compared to desktop computers. Uses of laptop computers Students use laptops for schoolwork and research. Business users use laptops for presentations and remote working. Laptops are used for internet access and communication while travelling. They are used for multimedia tasks such as watching videos. Teachers use laptops for lesson planning and delivery. Laptops can connect to wired or wireless networks to access shared resources like shared files, printers, and the internet. Advantages of laptop computers Laptop computers are portable and easy to carry. They can be used without a mains power supply for a period of time. All components are built into one device, reducing cable use. Wireless connectivity allows internet access in many locations. They require less space than desktop computers. Disadvantages of laptop computers Laptop computers are usually more expensive than desktops with similar performance. Components are difficult or impossible to upgrade. They have less powerful cooling systems. Battery life limits usage time away from mains power. Repairs can be more costly than for desktop computers. Single-board Computers A single-board computer is an entire computing system built on one circuit board. It contains the processor, memory, and ports for external hardware. These devices are commonly used to learn coding, set up small servers, or build robotics projects. They consume little power and take up very little physical space. The Raspberry Pi is a well-known model of this type of computer.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Locating Stored Files Storing Files: Hardware Computers store files on secondary storage devices like Solid State Drives (SSD) or Hard Disk Drives (HDD). SSD: a storage device that uses flash memory to store data, providing very fast file access speeds. HDD: a storage device that uses rotating magnetic platters and a moving read/write head to access data. Locating files on an SSD is much faster than an HDD because it has no moving parts to reposition. Folder Structures Users organise data by placing related files into specific digital folders. Folder: a virtual container within a computer's file system used to group files together. Hierarchical structures allow users to navigate through sub-folders to find specific information. Sub-folder: a folder contained within another folder, forming a nested organisational system. File Paths A file path describes the exact location of a file within the drive and folder hierarchy. File Path: a string of characters that specifies the unique location of a file or directory. This path usually starts with the drive letter and follows through each folder name separated by backslashes. Understanding the file path helps users identify where a document is saved on the hard drive. Search Tools Operating systems provide built-in search utilities to help users locate misplaced files. Search Utility: a software tool that scans the file system to find files based on specific criteria. Users enter keywords, file names, or extensions into the search bar to filter results. These tools can also search within the content of documents to find specific text strings. File Metadata Metadata provides additional details about a file that can be used for sorting and searching. Metadata: data that provides information about other data, such as the date created or file size. Users can filter files by the date they were last modified to find recent work. Sorting by file type allows users to quickly separate images from text documents.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > File Management

content.topicNotes: Log-ins and Passwords What is a User ID? A user ID is a unique identifier for a user. It identifies who is accessing a system. Each user has their own user ID. It is used together with a password for security. What is a Password? A password is a secret word or code. It is used to verify a user's identity. Only the authorised user should know it. It prevents unauthorised access to data. How They Work Together The user enters a user ID to identify themselves. The password confirms their identity. Authentication checks if the details are correct. Access is granted only when both match stored data. Systems may lock accounts after failed attempts. This helps against brute-force attacks. A brute-force attack is an automated hacking method where a computer repeatedly guesses every possible combination of letters, numbers, and symbols until it finds the correct password. Improving Security Strong passwords should be long and complex. Users should include uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Passwords should not be shared with others. Regular password changes improve security. Users should not reuse passwords across accounts. Security Questions Security questions ask personal facts to confirm identity during password resets. They provide an easy secondary recovery option if login credentials are forgotten. Answers can be weak if attackers easily discover them on social media. Avoid predictable responses and choose prompts with unique, obscure answers.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Potential Risks to Data & Personal Information

content.topicNotes: Lookups & External Data Sources Lookups & External Data Sources Spreadsheet lookup functions search for a specific value in a dataset and retrieve corresponding data from another row or column. External data sources refer to data stored outside the current worksheet or workbook, such as a separate file or database. Workbook: A spreadsheet file that contains one or more worksheets. For example, the formula =VLOOKUP(A2, '[Stock_Data.xlsx]Sheet1'!$A$2:$C$100, 3, FALSE) links directly to an external data file to pull a price. LOOKUP, HLOOKUP, VLOOKUP & XLOOKUP LOOKUP: Searches a single sorted row/column (vector) and returns a value from the same position in another vector. VLOOKUP: Searches vertically down a table's first column, moving right to retrieve data based on a column index number. HLOOKUP: Searches horizontally across a table's top row, moving down to retrieve data based on a row index number. XLOOKUP: Searches a specific range and returns a match from a second range in any direction. Lookup Functions Usage Examples =LOOKUP(101, A2:A4, B2:B4) finds ID 101 in a sorted vector and returns "Alice" from the result vector. =VLOOKUP(102, A2:D4, 2, FALSE) searches vertically down Column A for ID 102 and returns "Bob" from the second column. =HLOOKUP("Department", A1:D4, 4, FALSE) searches horizontally across Row 1 for "Department" and returns "Marketing" from Row 4. =XLOOKUP(103, A2:A4, D2:D4) matches ID 103 in Column A and returns the salary "£38,000" directly from Column D.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Spreadsheet

content.topicNotes: MAC Address What a MAC Address Is A MAC address uniquely identifies a device on a network. MAC stands for Media Access Control. The manufacturer assigns a MAC address to a NIC. A NIC is a Network Interface Card that connects a device to a network. How MAC Addresses Are Used A network uses MAC addresses to deliver data to the correct device. Switches read MAC addresses to forward data efficiently. A switch is a device that connects multiple devices on a LAN. LAN means Local Area Network. MAC Address Features A MAC address is usually shown as six pairs of hexadecimal numbers like this: 00:80:41:ae:fd:7e It is fixed and does not change when a device moves networks. This makes it different from an IP address. An IP address can change depending on the network.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Requirements for Connecting to a Network

content.topicNotes: Magnetic Tape Drives What is magnetic tape storage Magnetic tape storage uses a long strip of plastic coated with magnetic material. Data is stored as magnetised patterns representing binary values. Magnetic tape is a sequential access storage medium. Sequential access means data is read in order from the start of the tape. Magnetic tape is non-volatile storage. How a magnetic tape drive works A magnetic tape drive reads and writes data using a read/write head. The tape is wound between reels inside a cartridge. The tape moves past the read/write head during operation. The drive must wind the tape to the correct position before reading. Latency is the delay caused while the tape moves to the required location. Uses of magnetic tape drives Organisations use magnetic tape for long-term data backup. Banks archive financial records on magnetic tape. Large companies store disaster recovery backups off-site. Data centres use tape for large volumes of rarely accessed data. Tape storage is suitable for archival purposes. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of magnetic tape Magnetic tape has very low cost per gigabyte. Magnetic tape is suitable for large-scale backups. Disadvantages of magnetic tape Sequential access causes high latency. Data retrieval is slow compared to hard drives. Magnetic tape is unsuitable for frequently accessed data.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Storage

content.topicNotes: Mail Merge What is Mail Merge? Mail merge is a feature that creates many copies of a document. It is used to send the same message to many people at once. Each copy is personalised for a different person. It includes details personal to that recipient, such as their name or address. Mail merge saves time by avoiding typing the same letter many times. Common uses include bank statements, school reports and marketing letters. The Two Files Used in Mail Merge Mail merge always uses two files. The first is the main document. This holds the text that stays the same in every copy. The second is the data source. This holds the personal details that change for each person. Types of Data Source The data source can come from different types of file. It can be a word-processed document, such as a table in a word processor. It can be a spreadsheet, such as a file created in a spreadsheet application. It can also be a database document, such as a table stored in a database.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Word Processing

content.topicNotes: Mainframe Computers What are Mainframe Computers? Mainframe computers are powerful digital devices designed for high-capacity bulk data processing. They manage thousands of simultaneous transactions every second. Transaction processing is the real-time execution of individual commercial tasks. Large organisations use mainframe computers to process huge amounts of data quickly. Key Characteristics Mainframes provide high reliability and continuous availability for critical tasks. Reliability means the system runs continuously without failing or shutting down. Multiple processors handle intense computational workloads at the same time. Internal redundancy ensures the system stays operational during hardware repairs. Redundancy is the inclusion of extra components to prevent system failure. Real-World Uses Banks process millions of credit card transactions daily on mainframe systems. Hospitals store and access thousands of patient records securely. Data security involves protecting digital information from unauthorised access. Government departments process national census data and tax returns efficiently.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Malware & Viruses Risk of Downloaded Files Downloaded files may contain malware which is harmful software designed to damage systems. Files from unknown sources are higher risk. Opening infected files can spread viruses. Viruses are a type of malware that copies itself and spreads among files or devices. Trusted Sources Users should download files from trusted websites. A trusted source is a reliable and verified provider. Official websites reduce the risk of malware. Third-party sites may contain modified harmful files. Software Protection Anti-malware tools safeguard systems by actively monitoring activity to identify and block security threats. Antivirus software scans files before opening and detects and removes malicious software. Regular updates improve detection of new threats. Safe Behaviour Users should avoid clicking unknown download links. Email attachments from unknown senders should not be opened. Software should be kept up to date. This regularly fixes security weaknesses in systems.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Potential Risks to Data & Personal Information

content.topicNotes: Master Slides What is a Master Slide? The Master slide is the top slide in a hierarchy that controls the visual elements for all subsequent slides. A master slide acts as a design template that stores information about the default theme and layout of a presentation. Changes made to this slide automatically update every single slide in the file. Purpose of Master Slides Presenters use master slides to maintain a highly professional and consistent appearance throughout the presentation. This feature saves a massive amount of time when creating large slide decks. Slide deck: A collective group of slides that make up a complete presentation file. Users edit the design layout once rather than altering every slide individually. Information Held on Master Slides Master slides store static elements that must appear in the exact same position on multiple pages. These templates hold background configurations, colour schemes, and default font styles for headings. Software programs use placeholders to position text and dynamic data automatically. Placeholder: A pre-formatted container that holds content such as body text, slide numbers, and footers. Dynamic Master Placeholders Slide Number Placeholder: Automatically assigns sequential page numbers. Automated Date Placeholder: Displays a fixed date or today's date on every page. Footer Placeholder: Holds fixed text, like student details (Name, Candidate Number, Centre Number).
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Presentation

content.topicNotes: Digital Communication Methods Ways Digital Devices Communicate Digital devices send and receive data in four main ways. Satellite communication uses orbiting satellites to send signals across the globe. Broadcast communication sends signals from one point to many receivers. Examples include TV and radio. Wired communication uses physical cables to carry data. Wireless communication sends data through the air without cables. Wired Communication Wired communication uses cables to connect devices and carry data. Cables give a stable, reliable connection. Data travels fast with little interference. Interference means unwanted signals that disrupt data. Wired connections are common in offices, schools and homes. A drawback is that cables limit where you can place a device. Wireless Communication Wireless communication sends data through the air using radio waves. Devices can connect without cables. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are common wireless methods. Wireless links are flexible but have some drawbacks. Interference: other signals can disrupt the connection. Blockages: walls and objects can weaken the signal. Distance: signals get weaker the further from the source. Satellite and Broadcast Communication Satellite communication sends signals up to a satellite in orbit. The satellite then sends the signal back down to a receiver. It works over very long distances, even in remote areas. Broadcast communication sends one signal out to many devices at once. TV and radio are the main examples. Broadcast signals travel one way only: from sender to receiver.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Types of Digital Communications

content.topicNotes: Media Players What is a Media Player? A media player is a digital device used to play audio and video files. Media players can be hardware devices or software applications. They are designed to store, organise and play back digital media. Digital media includes music, films, photos and podcasts. Portable Media Players A portable media player is a small, handheld device for playing media on the go. An MP3 player stores and plays audio files in the MP3 format. An MP4 player can also play video files as well as audio. They use flash memory to store files without moving parts. Streaming Media Players A streaming media player connects a TV to the internet to play online content. Streaming means receiving media in real time without downloading it first. Examples include the Amazon Fire TV Stick and Apple TV. They use apps like Netflix, YouTube and Spotify to access content. Comparing Media Players Portable media players store files locally and do not need the internet. Streaming media players need an internet connection to access content. Portable players are better for offline use, such as exercising or travelling. Streaming players offer a wider range of content but rely on a good connection.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Digital Devices
ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Memory Cards What are memory cards A memory card is a small solid-state storage device. Memory cards store data using flash memory. Flash memory stores data electronically with no moving parts. Memory cards are non-volatile storage devices. Data is retained when power is switched off. Types of memory cards Common types include SD, microSD and CompactFlash cards. SD stands for Secure Digital. MicroSD cards are smaller versions of SD cards. Different devices require different card formats. Adapters allow smaller cards to fit larger slots. Uses of memory cards Digital cameras use memory cards to store photos and videos. Smartphones use memory cards to expand storage capacity. Tablets and handheld devices use memory cards for extra storage. Memory cards transfer files between devices. Portable devices rely on memory cards for lightweight storage. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Memory cards are very small and portable. Solid-state design makes memory cards resistant to shock. Disadvantages Memory cards are easy to lose due to small size. Storage capacity is lower than hard disks or SSDs.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Storage

content.topicNotes: Microphones and Sensors Microphone A microphone inputs sound and creates an analogue signal This electrical signal represents the original sound. An analogue signal varies continuously in voltage. An analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) changes the signal into digital data. Digital data uses binary values of 0 and 1. The computer stores or processes the digital sound. Sensors and analogue signals A sensor is an input device that detects physical changes such as temperature or light. Most sensors produce analogue signals. An analogue signal changes smoothly over a range of values. An ADC converts the analogue signal into digital form. The digital signal can then be processed by a microprocessor. Advantages and disadvantages of a microphone Advantages of a microphone A microphone allows voice input and communication. A microphone supports hands-free control and accessibility. Disadvantages of a microphone Background noise can reduce sound quality. A microphone may require additional hardware and software. Advantages and disadvantages of sensors Advantages of sensors Sensors provide continuous and automatic data collection. Sensors allow systems to respond quickly to environmental changes. Disadvantages of sensors Sensors can be expensive to install and maintain. Faulty or inaccurate sensors can cause incorrect system responses.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Input & Output

content.topicNotes: Microprocessor-Controlled Devices at Home What are microprocessor-controlled devices A microprocessor-controlled device uses a microprocessor to control its functions. A microprocessor is a small integrated circuit that processes instructions. Microprocessor-controlled devices follow programmed instructions automatically. Many household appliances contain microprocessors. Examples include washing machines, microwaves and smart thermostats. How the devices work Sensors (Input): Gather physical measurements from the surroundings, such as tracking temperature inside an oven or water levels in a washing machine. Microprocessor (Process): Evaluates incoming readings against preset user thresholds (for example, checking if the current temperature matches a target setting). Actuators (Output): Mechanical components triggered by the microprocessor to make physical changes, like starting a heating element or driving a drum motor. Advantages at home Microprocessor-controlled devices save time by working automatically. Tasks are completed more accurately and consistently. Energy efficiency is improved through precise control. Devices can improve safety with automatic shut-off features. Smart devices can be programmed to suit user needs. Disadvantages at home Microprocessor-controlled devices are often more expensive to buy. Repairs can be costly and require specialist knowledge. Faulty software can cause devices to malfunction. Users may become over-reliant on automation. Power cuts can stop devices from working. Examples in the home Washing machines use microprocessors to control wash cycles. Microwave ovens use microprocessors to control cooking time and power. Smart heating systems adjust temperature automatically. Dishwashers use sensors and microprocessors to control water use. Smart lighting systems allow automated control of lights.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Mobile Phones What is a smartphone A smartphone is a portable mobile computer that also functions as a telephone. It combines computing, communication and multimedia features in one device. Smartphones use a touch screen as the main input method. They run an operating system that supports apps. An app is a software application designed to perform a specific task. Uses of smartphones Smartphones are used for voice calls and text messaging. Users access the internet and social media on smartphones. Smartphones rely on SIM cards to connect to mobile networks. They are used for navigation using GPS. Smartphones are used for photography and video recording. Many people use smartphones for online banking and payments. Smartphones are used to remotely control devices e.g., smart home apps to adjust heating, flying drones etc. Advantages of smartphones Smartphones are highly portable and fit easily into a pocket. They provide constant internet access through mobile data or Wi-Fi. Built-in sensors support features such as cameras and fingerprint recognition. A wide range of apps makes smartphones very versatile. They combine multiple devices into one. Disadvantages of smartphones Smartphones have small screens that limit detailed work. Battery life restricts long-term use without charging. They are less powerful than laptops or desktop computers. Small keyboards can make typing difficult. Smartphones can be easily lost or stolen. Specialist Phones Specialist phones are built with features tailored to specific user needs. In general, they include various accessibility options to improve ease of use. A dedicated emergency button allows users to reach key contacts fast. High-volume speakers assist individuals with visual impairments.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Monitoring of Individuals What is Monitoring? Monitoring means tracking what a person does, where they go, or what they say. Digital technologies make it easy to collect this data automatically. Monitoring can happen without the person knowing. Monitoring Movements CCTV cameras record people in public places such as streets and shops. GPS (Global Positioning System) tracks a device's location in real time. Oyster cards and contactless payments log where and when a person travels. Monitoring Communications Emails, text messages and social media posts can all be monitored. Internet service providers (ISPs) can log which websites a user visits. An ISP is the company that connects you to the internet. Employers may monitor staff emails sent on work systems. Other Ways Individuals Are Monitored Cookies store data about websites you visit and items you search for. A cookie is a small file saved on your device by a website. Loyalty cards track what a customer buys in a shop. Smart devices such as voice assistants can record conversations. Why Monitoring Happens Governments may monitor people to prevent crime or terrorism. Companies monitor users to target them with adverts. Monitoring can improve safety but can also affect personal privacy. Privacy means the right to keep your personal data private.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Implications of The Use of Digital Technologies

content.topicNotes: Monitors What is a monitor A monitor is an output device that displays visual information from a computer. A monitor shows text, images, video and graphical user interfaces. The display updates as the computer processes data. Monitors allow users to see the results of their actions. Monitors are essential for most computer systems. Types of monitors LCD stands for Liquid Crystal Display. Liquid crystals change alignment to control light passing through the screen. LED stands for Light Emitting Diode. LED monitors are LCD monitors that use LED backlighting. LED is preferred over standard LCD: LED monitors offer brighter images, consume less power, have a longer lifespan, and allow the screen to be much thinner. Touch screen monitors combine display and input functions. Uses of monitors Monitors are used to view documents and web pages. Designers use monitors to edit images and videos. Teachers use monitors for presentations and demonstrations. Gamers use monitors for interactive entertainment. Control rooms use monitors to display live data. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of monitors Monitors provide immediate visual feedback. High-resolution screens improve image clarity. Large displays support detailed work. Disadvantages of monitors Prolonged use may cause eye strain. Large monitors require desk space. Power consumption increases with screen size.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Input & Output

content.topicNotes: Multifunctional Devices and Convergence What Does Multifunctional Mean? A multifunctional device can perform more than one task. It does several jobs in one piece of hardware. A mobile phone is a common example. It can make calls, take photos, play games, and use GPS. GPS (Global Positioning System) tracks your location using satellites. Having many functions in one device saves carrying several gadgets. Multifunctional Devices: Examples Modern mobile phones include a camera for taking photos and videos. They also have limited game-playing features built in. GPS lets the phone show maps and give directions. One device handles calls, photos, navigation, and games. This makes mobile phones a clear example of a multifunctional device. What is Convergence? Convergence means different devices start to share the same features. Their functions grow closer together over time. Smartphones and tablet computers are a key example. Both can browse the web, run apps, take photos, and stream video. It becomes harder to tell the two devices apart by what they do. Convergence happens as technology improves and devices gain more features. Convergence: Smartphones and Tablets Smartphones started as phones; tablets started as portable computers. Over time, both gained cameras, app stores, and mobile internet. Today, a smartphone and a tablet can do many of the same tasks. For example, both can video call, edit documents, and play games. This blurring of roles is what we call convergence.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Multimedia Projectors What are Multimedia Projectors? Multimedia or data projectors are output devices that project video and images onto a large screen. High-power light bulbs shine through internal lenses to form pictures. Features include zoom controls to adjust image size and high resolution for clarity. Compact, portable designs allow easy movement between locations. Common Uses of Projectors Displaying slideshows and lesson materials in classrooms and halls. Showing movies and live sports to large audiences in cinema spaces. Presenting business data and reports during professional meetings. Advantages and Disadvantages Advantages Produces very large display sizes for group viewing. Portable models allow easy transport between rooms. Takes up minimal desk space compared to large monitors. Disadvantages Ambient sunlight can reduce image brightness and quality. Replacement light bulbs are expensive to purchase. Cooling fans can produce background noise during use.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Input & Output

content.topicNotes: NFC What is NFC? NFC stands for Near Field Communication. Near Field Communication allows devices to exchange data over very short distances. Devices must be within 4 centimetres apart to communicate. How NFC Works An NFC-enabled device creates a small radio field. Another NFC device enters the field and establishes a connection. The devices exchange encrypted data. The system completes the process in a few seconds. Smartphone Payments Many smartphones contain built-in NFC chips. The user stores bank card details securely in a digital wallet app. The user taps the smartphone on a payment terminal. The system authorises the payment without inserting a physical card. Advantages and Security NFC works quickly and is easy to use. Transactions are executed quickly, and waiting times are reduced. The short range reduces the risk of unauthorised access. Encryption protects sensitive payment information. Users often confirm payments using fingerprint or face recognition. Disadvantages NFC only works over very short distances. Not all devices or payment terminals support NFC. Users may face security risks if they lose their smartphone. Interference from metal objects can reduce signal reliability.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Types of Digital Communications

content.topicNotes: Named Cells and Ranges Defining Named Cells and Ranges Users assign descriptive text labels to individual cells or blocks of adjacent cells. Named cell refers to a single cell identified by a custom descriptive text label instead of a letter-number coordinate. Named range refers to a group of selected cells identified collectively by a single custom text identifier. This custom identifier replaces standard absolute cell references like "$A$1:$B$10" in mathematical formulas. Purpose and Benefits Custom text identifiers make complex spreadsheet formulae significantly easier to read and audit. Formula auditing describes the process of checking mathematical expressions for structural correctness and logic. Named ranges automatically act as absolute references to prevent coordinates from shifting during replication. Creators use these meaningful names to simplify data model navigation and reduce syntax entry errors.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Spreadsheet

content.topicNotes: Navigation Aids What are Navigation Aids? Navigation aids are tools that help people find their way from one place to another. They can be physical devices or software applications. They use data such as location, speed and direction to guide users. Before digital aids, people used paper maps and compasses. What is GPS? GPS stands for Global Positioning System. It is a network of satellites that orbit the Earth. A GPS receiver picks up signals from these satellites. It uses the signals to work out your exact location on Earth. GPS works anywhere in the world, at any time of day. Uses of GPS and Navigation Aids In-car satellite navigation (sat nav) uses GPS to give turn-by-turn directions. Smartphones use GPS in map apps such as Google Maps. GPS helps delivery drivers plan the fastest routes. Walkers and cyclists use GPS devices to track their routes outdoors.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Peer-to-Peer and Client-Server Networks What is a Network? A network is two or more computers linked together to share data and resources. Networks can be wired or wireless. Two common types of network are peer-to-peer and client-server. Peer-to-Peer Networks In a peer-to-peer network, all computers have equal status. No single computer is in charge. Each computer can share its files and resources directly with others. Small homes or offices often use peer-to-peer networks. They are simple to set up and need no dedicated server. Advantages and Disadvantages of Peer-to-Peer Advantages: Easy and cheap to set up. No need for a specialist to manage the network. Disadvantages: Security is harder to control. Performance can slow down as more computers join. Backing up data is harder as files are spread across many computers. Client-Server Networks In a client-server network, computers have different roles. <- A server is a powerful computer that provides services to other computers. A client is a computer that requests those services from the server. Schools and businesses often use client-server networks. The Role of Servers A server stores shared files and controls access to the network. It handles tasks such as printing, email and web hosting. A file server stores and manages files for all clients. A print server manages print jobs sent by clients. An email server sends and receives emails for the network. Advantages and Disadvantages of Client-Server Advantages: Security is easier to manage from one central server. Data is backed up in one place. A network manager can control user access from the server. Disadvantages: If the server fails, clients may lose access to files and services. Servers are expensive to buy and need specialist staff to run them.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Types of Digital Communications

content.topicNotes: Network Operating Systems What is a Network Operating System? A network operating system (NOS) is software that manages a network. It controls how devices share resources and communicate. It runs on a server, a powerful computer that manages the network. Other devices on the network are called clients. The NOS lets the server control access to files, printers and the internet. What Does a Network Operating System Do? A NOS handles user accounts and passwords. It controls who can access files and resources. It manages shared storage so many users can save and read files. It also handles network security and monitors activity. Without a NOS, devices could not share resources on a network. Identifying Devices on a Network Every device on a network must be identified so data reaches the right place. There are several ways to identify a device. A device name is a human-readable label given to a device. Example: 'LIBRARY-PC-04' identifies a computer in a library. Other methods include IP and MAC addresses.

content.topicNotes: Networks: LAN, WAN and PAN Device-to-Device Communication Digital devices can send and receive data between each other. This is called device-to-device communication. Devices can connect directly to one other device. They can also connect through a network. A network is a group of devices linked together to share data. Local Area Network (LAN) A LAN connects devices over a small area. Examples: a school, an office, or a home. All devices in a LAN are usually in the same building. A LAN is often set up using cables or Wi-Fi. A school computer network is a common example of a LAN. Wide Area Network (WAN) A WAN connects devices over a large area. It can span cities, countries, or the whole world. A WAN links two or more LANs together. The internet is the largest example of a WAN. WANs often use telephone lines or satellite links. Personal Area Network (PAN) A PAN connects devices over a very short range. Usually within a few metres of a person. PANs are used to link personal devices together. A common example is connecting a phone to wireless earbuds via Bluetooth. Another example is a smartwatch syncing with a phone. Tethering Tethering lets one device share its internet connection with another. For example, a phone can share its mobile data with a laptop. The phone acts like a portable Wi-Fi hotspot. A hotspot is a point that provides wireless internet access. Tethering can also work through a USB cable or Bluetooth.

content.topicNotes: OMR and OCR Optical Mark Recognition (OMR) Optical Mark Recognition (OMR) detects shaded marks on paper forms. OMR reads ticks or filled circles in specific positions. OMR does not recognise printed text or handwriting. Specially designed forms are required for OMR. OMR is used for multiple-choice exam answer sheets. Uses of OMR Schools use OMR to mark exam papers quickly. Companies use OMR for customer satisfaction surveys. Election ballots can be processed using OMR. OMR reduces human marking errors. OMR saves time when processing large numbers of forms. Optical Character Recognition (OCR) Optical Character Recognition (OCR) converts scanned text into editable digital text. OCR recognises printed letters and numbers. A scanner or camera captures the original document. The software analyses character shapes. The output can be edited in a word processor. Examples of OCR Passport control/immigration services use OCR to read passport details instantly Post offices use OCR to read postal codes on envelopes. Apps use OCR to scan receipts and extract totals. Advantages and Disadvantages Advantages OMR processes forms quickly and accurately. OCR allows printed text to be reused digitally. Disadvantages OMR requires carefully completed forms. If a user creases/dirties the paper, or fails to circle completely with the correct pencil type the system will misread the data OCR may produce errors if the scan quality is poor.

content.topicNotes: Online & Local Services What are Online Services? Online services are services accessed over the internet. They run on remote servers, not on your own device. A server is a powerful computer that stores and sends data. Examples include web-based email, streaming sites, and cloud storage. You need an internet connection to use them. Features of Online Services Online services can be used from any device with internet access. Data is stored remotely, so you can reach it anywhere. They are often updated automatically by the provider. Many online services let several users work on the same file at once. This is called real-time collaboration. Examples of Online Services Web-based email (such as Gmail) lets you send and read messages via a browser. Cloud storage (such as Google Drive) saves files on remote servers. Video streaming (such as YouTube) plays media hosted on the internet. Online banking lets users manage accounts through a website or app. What are Local Services? Local services are services that run on your own device or local network. A local network links devices within one building. They do not need an internet connection to work. The software and data are stored on the device or a local server. Examples include a word processor installed on a PC. Features of Local Services Local services work without an internet connection. They are often faster, as data does not travel over the internet. The user controls where data is stored. Updates must be installed manually by the user or a network manager. Access is usually limited to devices on the local network. Comparing Online and Local Services Online services need the internet; local services do not. Online services store data on remote servers; local services store data nearby. Online services are easy to access from anywhere. Local services may be more secure, as data stays on a private network. Local services keep working if the internet goes down.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Online Goods and Services > Impact of Online Services

content.topicNotes: Online & Local Storage What is Data Storage? Data storage means keeping digital files so they can be used later. There are two main types: local storage and online storage. Local storage keeps data on a physical device near the user. Online storage keeps data on servers accessed via the internet. Local Storage Local storage holds data on a device you can physically touch. Examples include a hard disk drive (HDD), solid-state drive (SSD), USB flash drive, or optical disc. You can access local files without an internet connection. Local storage gives fast access to files. It has a fixed capacity set by the hardware. Files are at risk if the device is lost, stolen, or damaged. Users must back up files themselves to avoid losing data. Online Storage Online storage (also called cloud storage) saves data on remote servers. Remote servers are computers run by a provider in another location. Examples include Google Drive, OneDrive, and Dropbox. You need an internet connection to access online storage. Files are available anywhere in the world. Providers usually back up data automatically. Storage space can often be increased by paying for more. Comparing Online and Local Storage Local storage: fast access, no internet needed, fixed capacity. Online storage: access from anywhere, needs internet, flexible capacity. Online storage depends on the provider staying in business. Local storage gives the user full control over their data. Both types can be used together for extra security.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Online Goods and Services > Online Software

content.topicNotes: Online Gaming Safety Using Safe Usernames Players should use nicknames instead of real names for usernames when gaming online. A username is a name used to identify a player in a game. It should not include personal details such as age or location. This reduces the risk of strangers identifying or tracking the player. Protecting Personal Information Players should avoid sharing personal information in chats or profiles. Personal information includes data that identifies a person. Examples include full name, address, school, or phone number. Sharing this data can lead to identity theft or unwanted contact. Keeping Financial Details Secure Players should never share bank or payment details in games. Financial data includes card numbers, passwords, or account details. These details allow access to money or purchases. Scammers may pretend to offer rewards to steal this information. Recognising Online Risks Players should stay alert to suspicious behaviour from others, called scams.A scam is a trick designed to steal data or money. Scammers may offer fake prizes or pretend to be an official employee of the game's company and ask for login details. Players should report suspicious users to keep the gaming environment safe. Avoid unmonitored servers featuring offensive language or media. Immediately block and report players who cause distress or engage in cyberbullying.

content.topicNotes: Payment Methods Card Payments Customers pay using debit or credit cards. The card reader connects to an EFTPOS terminal. EFTPOS stands for Electronic Funds Transfer at Point of Sale. The bank authorises the transaction before the system completes the sale. Contactless and Mobile Customers tap a contactless card or smartphone on the reader. Contactless payment uses NFC. NFC stands for Near Field Communication. The device sends encrypted payment data to the bank. The system processes the payment in seconds. Third-Party Payment Systems Services like PayPal act as an intermediary between buyers and sellers. Users complete purchases without sharing bank details with merchants. Accounts link directly to bank cards or stored digital balances. This simplifies checkout while adding an extra layer of privacy. How Payments are Protected Encryption scrambles sensitive financial data during transmission. Two-factor authentication confirms user identity via secondary codes. Fraud detection tools monitor transactions for unusual activity. These safeguards prevent unauthorized access and financial theft.

content.topicNotes: Opening and Importing Files Opening Native Files Users open files when they want to access a document created in its original application. Native File: a file format that is unique to a specific software application, such as .docx for Microsoft Word. Double-clicking a file icon automatically launches the associated software to display the content. This process maintains all original formatting and specific features of the software. Importing External Data Importing allows users to bring data from one application into a different, currently open file. Import: the process of converting data from an external format into a format usable by the current application. A common example includes placing a .csv file into a spreadsheet to organise raw data. CSV (Comma Separated Values): a plain text file format used to store tabular data. Application Compatibility Many applications can open files created in different software if they share compatibility. Compatibility: the ability of one software program to correctly interpret and display the data from another. A user might use a word processor to open a file originally created in a different brand of office suite. Software often provides a 'Open File With' dialogue box to let users select the specific file type they wish to access.

content.topicNotes: Operating Systems What is an Operating System? An operating system is system software that manages computer hardware and software resources. The operating system provides a user interface to interact with the computer. The operating system controls tasks such as running programs and managing files. Key Functions Operating systems (OS) manage memory and allocate space for programs. OS schedule the CPU to run multiple programs efficiently. OS control input and output devices like keyboards and printers. Print spooling is used to queue documents for printing. OS provide security through user accounts and password protection. Single-user & Network Operating System Single-user OS lets one person interact with local files and programs at a time. Network OS connects computers to share files, devices, and security settings. Single-user OS suits personal devices, while network OS suits server environments. Examples of Operating Systems Windows is a common operating system used on many personal computers. macOS is the operating system for Apple Mac computers. Linux is an open-source operating system used in servers and some computers. Android and iOS are the most popular operating systems for mobile devices.

content.topicNotes: Page Size and Orientation Page Size Page size defines the physical dimensions of a document page. Common page sizes include A4 and A3. Users choose a page size based on the document purpose. Larger page sizes can show more content. Portrait Orientation Portrait orientation is taller than it is wide. It is often used for letters and reports. Portrait suits documents with mostly text. It helps text fit neatly down the page. Landscape Orientation Landscape orientation is wider than it is tall. It is useful for wide tables and charts. Landscape gives more space across the page. Users choose it when content needs extra width. Changing Layout Users can change page size and orientation in page setup. Page setup controls how a document appears when printed. Correct settings improve presentation. Good layout makes documents easier to read. Choosing the Best Option Users should match the page settings to the content. Reports often use A4 portrait orientation. Tables and diagrams may fit better in landscape. Careful choices improve document quality.

content.topicNotes: Practical Tips for Queries Query Criteria Operators The = symbol finds records matching an exact value. The <> symbol excludes specific values from results. Symbols like > and < filter numerical or date ranges. Symbols like >= and <= include boundary values in range checks. Wildcard Operator Rules An asterisk * replaces any amount of unknown text. Example: Like "A*" finds text starting with the letter A, such as "Austin" or "Atlanta". A question mark ? replaces just one character. Example: Like "P?t" matches words like "Pet", "Pit", or "Pot". Combining Search Criteria AND searches need records to match every condition. Put criteria on the same grid row for an AND search. OR searches need records to match at least one condition. Put criteria on separate grid rows for an OR search. Calculated Fields Calculated fields carry out math operations on existing fields during a query. Format: NewName: [Field1] * [Field2]. These fields update automatically when base data changes.

content.topicNotes: Personal Data Personal Data Characteristics Personal data includes information like a name, address, and date of birth. This data can identify an individual but may not always be sensitive. A photograph in a school uniform is also considered personal data. Sensitive Data Characteristics Sensitive data is a special type of personal data that includes medical history, religious beliefs, political opinions, biometric data (e.g., fingerprints), ethnic origin, or criminal records. This type of data requires extra protection due to its personal nature. Disclosing sensitive data without consent can lead to serious consequences. Need for Confidentiality Personal and sensitive data must be kept confidential to protect individuals. Unauthorised disclosure can result in identity theft or discrimination. Organisations must implement security measures to prevent leaks. Risks of Inappropriate Disclosure If personal data is shared without permission, it can be used maliciously. Schools and hospitals must ensure data is only accessible to authorised personnel. Failure to protect data can lead to legal penalties and loss of trust.

content.topicNotes: Pharming and Prevention What is Pharming? Pharming is a cyber attack that redirects users to fake websites. A cyber attack is an attempt to damage or access a computer system. Users may enter personal data without realising the site is fake. Attackers aim to steal sensitive data such as passwords. How Pharming Works Attackers reroute web traffic by placing malware onto a user's local storage drive. This may involve corrupting the Domain Name System (DNS) which translates web addresses into IP addresses. Users are redirected even if they type the correct address. Recognising Pharming Website appearance may look slightly unusual. Users should check for HTTPS in the address bar. This is often displayed by a padlock symbol next to the web address. HTTPS encrypts data between the user and the website. This converts data into a secure coded form. Users should check the complete domain name. Attackers could use similar domain names to the original, like "instapram.com" or "google.com.asuspiciousname.biz".
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Potential Risks to Data & Personal Information

content.topicNotes: Phishing and Prevention What is Phishing? Phishing is a scam where attackers trick users into giving personal data. A scam is a dishonest scheme used to steal information or money. Attackers often pretend to be trusted organisations. They aim to collect passwords, bank details or personal data. Email Phishing Attackers send fake emails that look official. Emails may contain links to fake websites. Users may be asked to enter personal information. These messages often create urgency to pressure users. Recognising Phishing Users should check the sender's email address carefully. Suspicious links should not be clicked. Poor spelling and grammar can indicate a phishing attempt. Unexpected requests for sensitive data should be treated as suspicious. Preventing Phishing Users should avoid clicking unknown links. Security software can detect malicious content. Two-factor authentication adds an extra layer of security. Users should verify requests directly with organisations. Two-Factor Authentication Two-factor authentication requires two forms of identification. It combines something you know and something you have. For example, a password and a code sent to a phone. This makes it harder for attackers to gain access.

content.topicNotes: Placing Images in Documents Importing Graphics Users place images into a document by using the 'Insert' or 'Import' function within the software. Importing: the process of bringing an external file into the current application. Software preserves the aspect ratio of the image to ensure it does not look stretched or squashed. Aspect Ratio: the proportional relationship between the width and the height of an image. Placing an image correctly ensures that the visual data aligns with the surrounding text. Placing Images with Precision Software allows users to place an image at an exact location using coordinates or alignment tools. Alignment: the positioning of an image relative to the margins or other objects on a page. Users can select horizontal and vertical alignment options such as top, bottom, left, or right. This ensures the graphic sits perfectly flush against the page edges without needing manual measurements. Precision tools help maintain a consistent and professional look across different pages of a document. Placing a Border Users can place a border around an image to make it stand out from the page background. Border: a decorative or solid frame that surrounds the edges of a graphic or image. Software tools allow for the adjustment of line weight, colour, and style for the frame. Line Weight: the thickness or width of a line, usually measured in points (pt). A border helps separate an image from surrounding text or similarly coloured elements.

content.topicNotes: Plagiarism What is Plagiarism? Plagiarism means using someone else's work and passing it off as your own. This includes text, images, ideas and code found online or in books. Plagiarism is dishonest and often against the rules of schools and the law. Copyright law protects original work. It gives the creator the right to control how their work is used. Copy and Paste Copy and paste means taking text or images directly from a source. You copy the content without changing it. You then present it as your own work. This is the most obvious form of plagiarism. Even if you copy just a sentence, it can still count as plagiarism. Rewriting Rewriting means changing some words in a source but keeping the same meaning. For example, swapping 'big' for 'large' in every sentence. The ideas still belong to the original author. Rewriting without crediting the source is still plagiarism. Crediting a source means stating where the information came from. Paraphrasing Paraphrasing means putting someone else's ideas into your own words. It goes further than rewriting — the sentence structure also changes. Paraphrasing is a useful skill, but it must be done honestly. You must still credit the original source. Without credit, paraphrasing counts as plagiarism. Avoiding Plagiarism Always state where information comes from. This is called citing or referencing your source. Use quotation marks around any words copied directly. Write ideas in your own words after reading and understanding them. Doing your own research and thinking helps you avoid plagiarism.

content.topicNotes: Pointing Devices What are pointing devices A pointing device is an input device used to control the on-screen pointer. The pointer is a visual indicator that shows the user’s position on the screen. Pointing devices allow users to select, move and open items. Pointing devices are commonly used with graphical user interfaces. Movement of the device controls movement of the pointer. Mouse A mouse is a handheld pointing device moved across a flat surface. Buttons allow users to select and interact with on-screen objects. A scroll wheel allows vertical or horizontal scrolling. Optical sensors detect movement. A mouse is widely used with desktop computers. Touchpad and trackpad A touchpad is a flat touch-sensitive surface used to control the pointer. A touchpad is commonly built into laptops. Finger movement controls the pointer on the screen. Gestures such as tapping and scrolling are supported. A touchpad reduces the need for an external mouse. Trackball and joystick A trackball controls the pointer using a rotating ball. The device remains stationary during use. A trackball is ideal for users with limited mobility or disability. Trackballs are useful for industrial or moving environments like a ship A joystick is moved in different directions to control movement. Joysticks are commonly used in games and simulations. These devices offer precise control in specific tasks. Advantages and disadvantages of a mouse Advantages of a mouse A mouse provides accurate and precise pointer control. A mouse is easy to learn and suitable for most tasks. Disadvantages of a mouse A mouse requires a flat surface to operate. Repetitive use can cause strain injury. Advantages and disadvantages of a touchpad Advantages of a touchpad A touchpad is compact and built into laptops. A touchpad does not require extra desk space. Disadvantages of a touchpad A touchpad can be less precise than a mouse. A small surface area can limit detailed control. Advantages and disadvantages of a trackball and joystick Advantages of a trackball and joystick A trackball requires minimal desk space. A joystick provides excellent directional control in simulations. Disadvantages of a trackball and joystick A trackball can become dirty and require cleaning. A joystick is not suitable for general office work.

content.topicNotes: Printers What is a printer A printer is an output device that produces a hard copy of digital data. A hard copy is a permanent physical print on paper. Printers output text, images and graphics. They are commonly connected to computers or networks. Printers are widely used in homes, schools and offices. Inkjet printers An inkjet printer sprays tiny droplets of ink onto paper. It produces high-quality colour prints. Inkjet printers are suitable for photos and graphics. They are usually inexpensive to buy. Ink cartridges can be expensive to replace. Laser printers A laser printer uses toner and heat to produce prints. Toner is a fine powder used instead of liquid ink. Laser printers are fast and efficient. They are suitable for high-volume printing. Text quality is usually very sharp. Advantages and disadvantages An advantage is that printers produce permanent records. An advantage is that printed documents are easy to share physically. A disadvantage is the cost of ink, toner and paper. A disadvantage is that printers require maintenance. Printing uses physical resources and energy. Dot-matrix printers A dot-matrix printer strikes an inked ribbon with tiny pins to impact paper. It produces hard copies using a matrix of dots. Dot-matrix printers are suitable for multi-part carbon copies and continuous stationery. They work reliably in harsh, dusty, or dirty environments. They are very loud, slow, and produce low-quality printouts.

content.topicNotes: Productivity Tools & Web Authoring Word Processing Software Word processing software allows users to create, edit, and format text documents. Users can change fonts, add images, and check spelling and grammar. Word processing software is commonly used for letters, reports, and essays. Spreadsheet Software Spreadsheet software organises data into rows and columns. Single data entries in these rows and columns are called cells. Users can perform calculations using formulas and functions. Spreadsheet software is often used for budgets, timetables, and data analysis. Database Management Systems A database management system (DBMS) is application software. It is used to create, store and manage databases. It organises data so it can be accessed efficiently. It allows users to search, sort and update records. Examples include Microsoft Access and MySQL. Web Authoring Software Used to design, construct, and publish websites. Combines text, graphics, and web code like HTML Includes preview tools to inspect page layout. Presentation Software Creates multimedia slide decks for business or educational presentations. Supports embedded images, audio, and transitions. Used for delivering speeches and lectures. Project Management Software Plans schedules, tracks resources, and oversees progress. Displays project timelines through Gantt charts. Helps teams assign tasks and meet key deadlines.

content.topicNotes: Proofreading Checking Layout Proofreading is the process of reviewing a document for errors. Users should check the overall layout and presentation. They should identify formatting mistakes before publication. Careful proofreading improves document quality. Line Spacing and Blank Pages Users should check that line spacing is consistent.Line spacing is the vertical distance between lines of text. Blank pages or slides should be removed if unnecessary. Consistent spacing improves readability. Checking Styles Users should ensure styles are applied consistently.A style is a predefined set of formatting settings. Incorrect fonts, colours or spacing should be corrected. Consistent styles improve readability. Tables and Lists Tables must fit within column boundaries, fully showing all cell contents. Header rows must repeat at the top when a table splits across a page break. Bulleted lists need uniform symbols and precise margin or indent alignment. Item spacing must remain consistent, leaving space after the final item. Benefits of Software Tools Automated tools save time when checking documents. They help improve accuracy and consistency. Professional documents should contain as few errors as possible. Proofing tools support, but do not replace, human checking.

content.topicNotes: Purpose of Communication Software What is Communication Software? Communication software lets people exchange files and messages between computers or users. Messages can be sent as text, images, audio, or video. Communication softwar also provides remote access to systems. Remote access means connecting to another computer from a different location. Web Browsers A web browser is software used to access and view websites. It lets users retrieve and display web pages from the internet. Examples include Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, and Microsoft Edge. Email Email (electronic mail) lets users send messages between computers over a network. Messages can include text, images, and file attachments. Email is used for both personal and business communication. Social Media and Instant Messaging Social media platforms let users share text, images, audio, and video with others. Examples include Instagram, X (formerly Twitter), and Facebook. Instant messaging lets users send and receive text messages in real time. Examples include WhatsApp and Snapchat. SMS and MMS SMS (Short Message Service) lets users send short text messages between mobile phones. MMS (Multimedia Messaging Service) lets users also send images, audio, and video. Both use mobile networks to deliver messages.

content.topicNotes: Remote Control, Joysticks and Driving Wheels Remote control A remote control is an input device used to control a system from a distance. A remote control sends signals using infrared or radio waves. Infrared requires a clear line of sight between devices. Remote controls are commonly used with televisions and media systems. Buttons allow users to select options and control functions. Joystick A joystick is an input device that is moved in different directions. Movement controls an on-screen object or cursor. Joysticks often include buttons for additional actions. Joysticks are commonly used in control systems and simulators. A joystick provides precise directional control. Driving wheel A driving wheel is an input device designed to simulate steering. A driving wheel is mainly used in driving and racing simulations. Turning the wheel controls steering in the software. Pedals are often included for acceleration and braking. Driving wheels increase realism and user immersion. Advantages and disadvantages a remote control Advantages of a remote control A remote control allows operation from a distance. A remote control is simple and easy to use. Disadvantages of a remote control Infrared remote controls require line of sight. Limited input options are available. Advantages and disadvantages a joystick Advantages of a joystick A joystick provides precise directional control. A joystick enhances gaming and simulation experiences. Disadvantages of a joystick A joystick is not suitable for typing or general tasks. A joystick is mainly designed for specific applications. Advantages and disadvantages a driving wheel Advantages of a driving wheel A driving wheel provides realistic steering control. A driving wheel improves immersion in racing simulations. Disadvantages of a driving wheel A driving wheel requires additional space and hardware. A driving wheel is limited to specialised software.

content.topicNotes: Repetitive Strain Injury and Back Problems Repetitive strain injury (RSI) Repetitive strain injury (RSI) is damage to muscles, tendons or nerves. RSI is caused by repeated movements over long periods. Common activities include typing or using a mouse. Symptoms include pain, stiffness and tingling. RSI can worsen without proper rest or posture. Causes of RSI Continuous keyboard or mouse use can strain muscles. Poor workstation setup increases the risk of injury. Lack of breaks prevents muscles from recovering. Incorrect hand or wrist position causes stress. High repetition tasks increase strain on joints. Back problems Back problems are caused by poor sitting posture. Sitting for long periods puts pressure on the spine. An unsupportive chair increases strain on the back. Incorrect screen height can lead to slouching. Back pain can become long-term if not corrected. Prevention methods Regular breaks reduce strain on muscles and joints. An adjustable chair supports correct posture. The keyboard and mouse should be positioned correctly. Use of ergonomic keyboards and mice improves wrist alignment and reduces finger strain. Screen height should be at eye level. Stretching exercises help prevent injury.
