content.topicNotes: Report Data in Databases What are Reports? Database reports present information from a table or query in a structured, professional layout. A query is a search or filter applied to a database to retrieve specific data. Reports organise data so that humans can easily read and understand the findings. Users design reports to summarise large amounts of data for presentation. Purpose and Importance Managers use reports to make informed business decisions based on accurate data trends. Reports distribute key data to stakeholders who do not have direct access to the database. Database software automates the reporting process to save time and reduce human error. Users add headers, footers, and page numbers to make the data look professional. Access vs Word Processors Microsoft Access links reports directly to dynamic data for real-time updates across records. Dynamic data means database information that updates automatically when changes occur. Word processors require manual data entry and suit static, text-heavy narrative documents. Choose Access to easily sort, group, and calculate large volumes of relational database data. Access Reports Structure The "Report Header" and "Report Footer" display information only once at the absolute start and end of the document. The "Page Header" and "Page Footer" display repeating details at the top and bottom of every individual page. The "Detail" section contains the actual data fields and records retrieved from the database. Records represent individual rows of structured data stored within a database table. Mail Merge Documents Mail merge combines a master document with a database source automatically. Software inserts record fields, like names, into placeholder merge tags. It produces personalised batch letters or invoices rapidly without manual typing. Schools use mail merge to send customized documents to students. Practical Tips for Reporting Data Sorting and Grouping Data Sorting places records in alphabetical or numerical order. Multi-level sorting sorts by a main field, then a secondary field. Grouping collects related records under one main header. Grouping lets you run summary calculations for each distinct category. Summary Calculations Aggregate functions compute summary statistics across all listed records. Examples include =SUM() for totals, =AVG() for averages, and =COUNT() for totals counts. Put controls in the Report Footer for overall totals. Put controls in a Group Footer for category totals. Report Formatting Checklist Match page setup (Portrait/Landscape) so data does not overflow pages. Make sure all labels and values display clearly without truncation or ### errors. Add student details (Name, Candidate Number, Centre Number) in headers or footers. Display a clear main title once at the top in a large font.

content.topicNotes: Responsible Use & Behaviour Policies What is a Responsible Use Policy? A responsible use policy is a set of rules for how members must behave online. It is sometimes called an acceptable use policy (AUP). The policy tells members what they can and cannot do. It helps keep the community safe and fair for everyone. Purpose of These Policies The main purpose is to protect members from harm. Policies stop bullying, harassment, and offensive content. They also protect personal data and user privacy. Following the rules helps the community stay a positive place. What the Policies Cover Policies set rules on the type of content members can post. They ban hate speech, threats, and illegal content. They explain how to report rule-breaking behaviour. They also cover how the platform will deal with those who break the rules. Consequences of Breaking the Rules Members who break the rules may get a warning. Their content may be removed by moderators. A moderator is a person who checks and manages content. Repeated rule-breaking can lead to a ban from the community. Some actions may even be reported to the police.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Use of Online Communities

content.topicNotes: Reviewing Digital Products Against Requirements What Does 'Reviewing a Digital Product' Mean? A digital product is any file or output made using software. Examples include a poster, a spreadsheet or a database. Reviewing means checking the finished product against the original requirements. Requirements are the goals set at the start of a project. This tells you whether the software did what was needed. What Are Original Requirements? Original requirements are the list of things the product must do or include. They are agreed upon before work begins. Examples of requirements: correct file format right audience and purpose specific features, such as a company logo or working formulas. You compare the finished product against each requirement in turn. How to Compare Product with Requirements Go through each requirement one by one. Ask: does the product meet this requirement? If yes, the outcome is a success for that point. If no, note what is missing or wrong. This gives clear evidence of what the software achieved. Outcomes of Using Software Applications An outcome is the result of using a software application. Outcomes can be: fully met: the product matches the requirement. partly met: some features are correct, but others are missing. not met: the requirement was not achieved at all. Recording outcomes helps you improve the product. Why Reviewing Against Requirements Matters Reviewing against requirements shows whether the software was used correctly and effectively. It highlights mistakes or missing features. It gives a basis for making improvements. A good review is specific and refers to exact requirements.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Applying Information and Communication Technology > Reviewing Outcomes

content.topicNotes: Risks of Using the Internet Undesirable and Offensive Content Users may accidentally or intentionally access undesirable content that is offensive, illegal, or harmful. This category includes criminal material, websites that contain harmful information, and cyberbullying. Cyberbullying: the use of digital platforms to send threatening or hurtful messages to intimidate others. Schools and parents often use filtering software to prevent exposure to these specific categories of websites. Phishing and Data Risks Fraudulent emails and websites use phishing techniques to trick users into revealing sensitive personal data. Phishing: the use of fake communications to gain personal information like passwords or credit card numbers. Stolen personal data often leads to identity theft, where criminals use the information for financial fraud. Avoiding the disclosure of personal details on public platforms helps to prevent targeted scams or security risks. Malware and Viruses Downloading files or clicking suspicious links can infect a computer with malicious software. Malware: software specifically designed to disrupt, damage, or gain unauthorised access to a computer system. These programs can delete files, steal data, or allow hackers to take control of hardware. Maintaining updated anti-virus software allows systems to detect and remove these threats effectively. Safety Precautions Individuals can protect accounts by using strong, unique passwords and enabling two-factor authentication. Schools and companies often implement robust firewalls and filtering software to monitor and block harmful traffic. Firewall: a security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on safety rules. Organisations provide regular training to help people recognise phishing attempts and secure their personal data.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Use of Online Communities

content.topicNotes: Risks to Data and Information What Are Risks to Data? Data is the raw facts stored on a computer system. Information is data that has been given meaning. Both can be lost, damaged or stolen. There are three main risks: accidental deletion, unauthorised access and hacking. Accidental Deletion Accidental deletion means data is removed by mistake. This can happen when a user deletes the wrong file. It can also happen due to a system crash or power cut. Once deleted, data may be very hard to recover. Regular backups help protect against this risk. Unauthorised Access Unauthorised access means someone views or changes data without permission. For example, a student reading a teacher's private files. It can happen inside an organisation, not just from outside. Strong passwords and user accounts help prevent this. Access controls limit who can see or edit data. Hacking Hacking means breaking into a computer system without permission. A hacker is someone who does this, often from a remote location. Hackers may steal, alter or destroy data. They can also install harmful software on the system. Firewalls and encryption help protect against hacking. Why These Risks Matter Data loss can harm people and organisations. Personal data, such as bank details, can be misused if stolen. Businesses may lose money or face legal trouble. It is important to know these risks to put the right safeguards in place.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Potential Risks to Data & Personal Information

content.topicNotes: Rotating and Reflecting Images Rotating Images Users rotate an image to change its orientation by a specific number of degrees. Rotation: the process of turning an image around a central pivot point. Software allows for fixed rotations, such as 90 or 180 degrees, or free rotation to any angle. This tool helps correct photos taken at the wrong angle or fits graphics into specific layout spaces. Reflecting Images Users reflect an image to create a mirror image of the original graphic. Reflection: the process of flipping an image over a vertical or horizontal axis. Flipping an image horizontally reverses the left and right sides, which is useful for changing the direction a subject faces. Flipping an image vertically creates a top-to-bottom reversal, often used to create a water-like mirror effect. Choosing the Right Axis Axis: an imaginary line around which an object can rotate or be reflected. X-axis: flips the image vertically (top to bottom). Y-axis: flips the image horizontally (left to right). Z-axis: rotates the image flat against the screen (like a wheel spinning). X or Y rotation creates 3D-like tilt effects. Choosing the wrong axis may result in upside-down text or a perspective that looks unnatural to the viewer, thus reducing presentation quality.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Graphics

content.topicNotes: SSD, Pen Drive and Flash Drive What is solid-state storage Solid-state storage stores data using electronic memory chips. No moving parts are used to store or access data. Data is stored as binary values. Binary values use 0s and 1s to represent information. Solid-state storage is non-volatile. Solid-State Drive (SSD) A solid-state drive (SSD) is used as main backing storage in computers. An SSD uses flash memory instead of spinning disks. Data access speeds are very fast. SSDs are commonly used in laptops and modern desktop computers. Faster boot times improve system performance. Pen drive and flash drive A pen drive is a small portable solid-state storage device. A flash drive connects to a computer using a USB port. Flash memory refers to non-volatile storage chips that retain data when the power is turned off. Pen drives are used to transfer files between computers. Storage capacity varies from small to very large sizes. Flash drives are easy to carry and reuse. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Solid-state devices are fast and reliable. No moving parts reduce the risk of physical damage. SSDs consume less power and generate less heat, as they have no spinning parts, which extends battery life and keeps devices cooler Disadvantages Solid-state storage is more expensive per gigabyte. Limited write cycles can reduce lifespan over time.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Storage

content.topicNotes: Saving Files The Save Command Users use the Save command to update an existing file with the latest changes. Save: an operation that overwrites the current version of a file stored on a storage device. This process replaces the original data with the new version held in the computer's memory. It ensures that work is not lost if the application closes or the power fails. The Save As Command The Save As command allows users to create a new version of a file while keeping the original unchanged. Save As: a function that lets a user specify a new filename, file format, or storage location. This is useful for creating templates or saving documents in different formats for compatibility. File Format: a standard way that information is encoded for storage in a computer file. Version Control Version Control is the practice of tracking and managing changes to software code or documents. Saving files with unique names or timestamps helps users manage different stages of a project. Users can revert to an older version if a mistake occurs in the current working document. This prevents the accidental loss of data that might occur when overwriting a single file repeatedly. Naming Files File naming is the process of assigning descriptive and structured names to digital documents. Users apply naming conventions like version numbers and snake_case to format files safely. Snake case replaces spaces with underscores (_) to keep filenames readable and system-compatible. Proper naming ensures files remain easy to locate, organize, and open across different operating systems. An example is saving a file as project_report_v01.docx instead of document.docx.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > File Management

content.topicNotes: Scanners What are Scanners? A scanner is an input device used to convert paper documents into digital format. A scanner captures images of text or pictures. A scanner outputs a digital image Scanners are commonly used to digitise documents and photos. Uses of scanners Scanners are used to archive paper documents digitally. Scanners are used to input photographs into a computer. Offices use scanners to share documents electronically. Scanned text can be edited using OCR software. OCR stands for Optical Character Recognition and converts images of text into editable text. Scanners reduce the need for physical storage. Advantages and disadvantages of a scanner Advantages of a scanner A scanner creates accurate digital copies of documents. A scanner allows paper documents to be stored electronically. Disadvantages of a scanner Scanned images can create large file sizes. A scanner requires additional hardware and space.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Input & Output

content.topicNotes: Search Engines Finding Information Search engines help users find specific information from the billions of pages on the World Wide Web. They act as a massive digital directory that users can search instantly using keywords. Keywords: simple words or phrases that describe the main topics of a search. Without search engines, users would need to know the exact URL of every website they wanted to visit. Indexing The search engine organises collected data into a massive database known as an index. Index: a structured database that stores information about web pages to allow for fast retrieval. It stores keywords, metadata, and page descriptions to help categorise each site. Metadata: data that provides information about other data, such as tags or descriptions in a website's code. Search Queries and Ranking Users input a search query to find specific information within the search engine's index. Search Query: the specific words or phrases that a user enters into a search engine. Complex algorithms rank the results based on relevance and website authority. Algorithm: a process or set of rules followed in calculations or problem-solving operations. Result Retrieval The search engine displays the most relevant matches as a list on a results page. It provides a title, a brief snippet of text, and a URL for each identified web page. Users click on these links to navigate directly to the external website stored on a web server.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Availability & Use of Online Information

content.topicNotes: Securing Data on Networks Strong Passwords A strong password is difficult for others to guess. Users should include letters, numbers and symbols. Password length should be at least 8 characters. Avoid using personal information such as names or birthdays. Encryption Encryption converts data into a coded format. Only authorised users can decrypt the data. Decryption changes coded data back into readable form. This protects data if it is intercepted. Firewalls A firewall monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic. It blocks unauthorised access to a system by inspecting incoming and outgoing data against predetermined security rules. Firewalls can be hardware or software. They act as a barrier between a trusted network and the internet. User Access Levels Access levels control what users can see or do. An administrator is a user with full control of a system. Standard users have limited permissions. This reduces the risk of accidental or malicious changes. Transaction Logs & Backups Backups store separate copies of files to prevent data loss from disasters. Transaction logs record every database change in chronological order. Combining both tools allows systems to recover quickly after critical failures. Choosing Context-Specific Security Organizations select defenses based on their specific operating needs. Online shops combine encryption, firewalls, and complex passwords for payment safety. Offices use access tiers, transaction logs, and backups to protect internal files.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Connectivity > Securing Data on Networks

content.topicNotes: Selecting Appropriate Software Applications Word Processing Software Word processing software lets you create, edit and format text documents. Example: Microsoft Word or Google Docs. Use it for letters, reports, essays and other text-based documents. Features include spell check, font styling and page layout tools. Spreadsheet Software Spreadsheet software stores data in rows and columns called cells. Example: Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets. Use it for budgets, calculations, charts and data analysis. It can perform formulas automatically, such as adding up a column of numbers. Database Management Software Database management software stores and organises large amounts of data. Example: Microsoft Access. Use it to search, sort and filter records quickly. It is good for stock lists, customer records and school timetables. Presentation Software Presentation software lets you create slideshows with text, images and video. Example: Microsoft PowerPoint or Google Slides. Use it to present information to an audience. It is also called multimedia software because it combines different media types. Web Authoring Software Web authoring software lets you create and publish websites. Examples include Adobe Dreamweaver and WordPress. You can add text, images, links and video to a page. Some tools let you design visually, without writing code. This is called a WYSIWYG editor (What You See Is What You Get). Graphics Software Graphics software lets you create and edit images on a computer. Example: GIMP or Adobe Photoshop. There are two main types: bitmap and vector graphics software. Bitmap software edits images made of pixels. A pixel is a tiny coloured dot; photos are bitmap images. Vector software creates images from mathematical shapes and lines. Vector images stay sharp at any size.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Applying Information and Communication Technology > Software Applications

content.topicNotes: Social Impacts of Technology on Individuals What Are Social Impacts? Social impacts are the effects that technology has on people and society. Technology connects people across the world. It changes how people communicate, work, and spend their free time. These changes can be positive or negative. Reduced Social Interaction Many people now communicate online instead of meeting in person. This can reduce face-to-face social interaction. Spending long periods online can lead to loneliness. People may feel less connected to those around them in real life. Cyberbullying Cyberbullying means using technology to harass or harm others. It can happen on social media, in messages, or in online games. It is harder to escape than face-to-face bullying. Victims can be targeted at any time, even at home. Wider network access increases the risk of cyberbullying. Less-Restricted Access to Networks People can now access networks at any time, from almost anywhere. Mobile devices such as smartphones let users stay connected all day. This makes it easy to share and view content without restriction. It also means harmful or illegal content can spread more easily. Changes in Ways of Socialising Technology has changed how people form and keep friendships. Social media platforms let users share updates with large groups. Online communities allow people with shared interests to connect. Some people find it easier to socialise online than in person. Balancing the Impacts Technology brings both benefits and risks to society. Benefits include staying in touch with family and friends far away. Risks include reduced real-world interaction and cyberbullying. Society must find ways to manage these impacts safely.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Impact of The Internet on Individuals

content.topicNotes: Social Media Blocking and Reporting Users should block unwanted contacts to stop communication. This prevents a person from viewing or messaging your profile. Users should report harmful behaviour to platform moderators, so the service provider is alerted to rule-breaking content. These tools help maintain a safer online environment. Meeting Online Contacts Underage users must avoid meeting online contacts without adult supervision. Online contacts may not be who they claim to be. In some cases someone builds trust to exploit a young person, this is called Grooming. Always inform a trusted adult before any meeting. Meeting strangers alone increases personal safety risks. Responsible Sharing Users should not share inappropriate images or messages, including offensive, sexual, or harmful material. Users must respect others' personal data and privacy. Users should communicate respectfully and avoid offensive language. Posts, comments, and media published online leave a lasting digital footprint that can be viewed indefinitely.

content.topicNotes: Software Licencing Protecting Software Developers issue a formal agreement to specify how many users can install the application. Software Licence: a legal instrument governing the use or redistribution of software. Companies use multi-user licences to allow a specific number of employees to access the program legally. Users must agree to the terms of the End User Licence Agreement (EULA) before installation. Technical Protection Methods Systems require a unique product key to verify that the user purchased a legitimate copy. Product Key: a specific alphanumeric code used to register or activate a software program. Software communicates with an online server to prevent duplicate installs. Physical security devices like dongles must be plugged into a USB port for some specialist software to function. Program code is converted into executable format and encrypted to prevent unauthorized viewing or editing. Anti-Piracy Measures Programmers include code that checks for the presence of the original physical disc during startup. Developers release regular updates that verify the software's authenticity over the internet. Digital Rights Management (DRM): technologies used to control the use, modification, and distribution of copyrighted works. Software identifies and blocks 'cracked' versions to ensure only paying customers have access. Free and Open Source Software Free and open source software gives users the freedom to study, adjust, and share the source code without paying fees. Source code is made public so anyone can inspect and modify it to fix bugs or add new features. Users can redistribute altered versions to help the wider community. Linux and LibreOffice are popular real-world examples.

content.topicNotes: Software Updates Why Software is Updated Software updates are new versions of a program released by developers. Updates fix vulnerabilities. A vulnerability is a weakness that hackers can exploit to attack a system. Updates fix bugs. A bug is an error in the code that causes the software to behave incorrectly. Updates can also improve performance and efficiency. More Reasons for Updates Updates improve compatibility. Compatibility means the software works correctly with other programs or devices. Updates add new features to make software more useful. Updates improve usability. Usability means how easy the software is to use. How Updates are Delivered Updates are downloaded from a server run by the software developer. Automatic scheduling allows the computer to check for and install updates on its own. This keeps software up to date without the user needing to act. Manual updates require the user to download and install the update themselves. Risks of Updating Software Updates can sometimes cause problems. A new update may make software incompatible with other programs. An update could contain new bugs or errors. In rare cases, an update can corrupt or delete data. It is important to back up your system and files before installing an update. A backup is a copy of your data stored safely elsewhere.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Software

content.topicNotes: Speakers What are speakers Speakers are output devices that produce sound from a computer. Speakers convert digital audio data into sound waves. Sound waves are vibrations that can be heard by humans. Speakers allow users to hear music, speech and alerts. Speakers are commonly connected to computers, phones and tablets. How speakers work The computer sends digital audio signals to the sound system. A DAC converts digital signals into analogue signals. DAC stands for Digital Analogue Converter. An amplifier increases the strength of the analogue signal. A diaphragm and cone vibrate to create sound waves. Uses of speakers Speakers are used to listen to music and audio files. Video conferencing systems use speakers for voice output. Games use speakers to produce sound effects. Public address systems use speakers to reach large audiences. Accessibility tools use speakers for audio feedback. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of speakers Speakers provide clear audio output for multiple users. Speakers improve the multimedia experience. Disadvantages of speakers Loud audio can disturb other people. Sound quality varies depending on speaker design. External speakers require additional space and power.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Input & Output

content.topicNotes: Spelling, Punctuation & Grammar Spell Check Spell check identifies words that may be spelt incorrectly. It compares words against a built-in dictionary. A dictionary is a list of recognised words. Users should review suggestions before accepting changes. Punctuation Check Identifies missing or misplaced punctuation marks such as commas, full stops, and apostrophes. Flags issues like missing capital letters at the start of sentences or missing question marks. Ensures sentence structures are clear and accurate, preventing misunderstandings. For example, it highlights a missing apostrophe in 'its' when 'it's' (it is) is intended. Grammar Check Grammar check identifies possible grammar mistakes. The tool may suggest improvements to sentence construction. Users should check that suggestions make sense. For example, it would suggest replacing 'me and my friend went out' with 'my friend and I went out'. Making Appropriate Changes Users should not accept every suggestion automatically. Some correct words may be flagged as errors. Technical terms may not appear in the dictionary. Users should apply changes only when appropriate.

content.topicNotes: Storage Devices, Media & Units Storage Devices and Storage Media A storage device is the hardware that reads and writes data. Example: a hard disk drive or an optical disk drive. Storage media is the material that actually holds the data. Example: a magnetic disk or a Blu-ray disc. The device and the media are not the same thing. Some devices have built-in media (e.g. an SSD). Others use removable media (e.g. a DVD in an optical drive). What Is Backing Storage Backing storage stores data and programs permanently. It is also called secondary storage. Backing storage keeps data when the power is turned off. Computers use it to save files and software. Bits, Bytes and Storage Units A bit is the smallest unit of data. It holds a 0 or a 1. A byte is 8 bits. Storage is measured in multiples of bytes. These multiples use powers of 1024 (not 1000). 1 kibibyte (KiB) = 1024 bytes. 1 mebibyte (MiB) = 1024 KiB. 1 gibibyte (GiB) = 1024 MiB. 1 tebibyte (TiB) = 1024 GiB. Hard Disk Drives A hard disk drive (HDD) uses magnetic storage. Magnetic storage uses magnetism to store data. HDDs offer large storage capacity at low cost. They contain moving parts that can wear out. Solid State Drives A solid state drive (SSD) uses flash memory. Flash memory stores data electronically with no moving parts. SSDs are faster than HDDs. They are more durable but usually cost more. Optical Storage Optical storage uses lasers to read and write data. Examples include CDs, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. They are portable and easy to distribute. Optical discs store less data than HDDs or SSDs.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Peripheral Devices - Storage

content.topicNotes: Sustainability Issues in Digital Technology What is Sustainability in ICT? Sustainability means meeting our needs today without harming the planet for future generations. Digital devices use energy and materials. This use can damage the environment. Understanding the impact helps us make better choices. ICT sustainability looks at how we make, use and dispose of digital devices. Environmental Impact: Energy Use Digital devices need electricity to run. Data centres (large buildings full of servers) use huge amounts of power. They run 24 hours a day, every day. Streaming video and browsing the internet all use energy. Most of this electricity still comes from burning fossil fuels. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which drives climate change. Environmental Impact: Manufacturing Making digital devices requires raw materials such as metals and plastics. Rare earth metals (hard-to-find minerals used in circuit boards and batteries) must be mined. Mining can destroy habitats and pollute water. Manufacturing factories also use large amounts of energy. Devices are replaced often, so demand for new materials stays high. Environmental Impact: E-Waste E-waste means old or broken electronic devices that are thrown away. E-waste is one of the fastest-growing waste problems in the world. Old devices can release toxic chemicals into soil and water if sent to landfill. Toxic chemicals include lead, mercury and cadmium. Much e-waste is shipped to developing countries, causing harm there. Mitigating the Impact: Greener Energy Using renewable energy (power from sources that do not run out, such as solar or wind) cuts carbon emissions. Data centres can be powered by renewable energy. Buying electricity from green energy suppliers reduces a device's carbon footprint. Carbon footprint means the total greenhouse gases produced by an activity. Mitigating the Impact: Responsible Use and Disposal Keeping devices longer reduces the need to manufacture new ones. Repairing a device instead of replacing it saves materials and energy. Recycling old devices recovers valuable metals and reduces toxic waste. Many shops and councils offer device recycling schemes. Buying refurbished (second-hand but tested) devices also helps.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Operating Online > Implications of The Use of Digital Technologies

content.topicNotes: System & Application Software Definition & Overview System software manages hardware and runs the computer. Application software lets users carry out specific tasks. System software creates the base for application software to function. System Software Its purpose is to control computer hardware and keep the system operating smoothly. It runs in the background to handle fundamental operations. Examples include operating systems like Windows, utility programs, and device drivers. Utility software performs maintenance tasks such as backup or compression of files. Application Software Application software is used to help end users perform specific tasks efficiently. Users interact directly with application software for work or entertainment. Examples include word processors, spreadsheets, image editors, and web browsers.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Software

content.topicNotes: System Configuration for User Needs What is System Configuration? System configuration means changing the settings of an ICT system. This makes the system work better for a specific user. Settings can be changed in both hardware and software. The right configuration helps a system meet the needs of its users. Display Settings Display settings control how content looks on screen. Users can increase text size to make reading easier. Screen resolution can be adjusted to make items larger or clearer. Colour contrast can be changed to help users with visual impairments. A visual impairment is a condition that affects a person's sight. Audio Settings Audio settings control sound on a device. Volume can be raised or lowered to suit the user. Sounds can be replaced with visual alerts for users who are deaf or hard of hearing. Text-to-speech reads on-screen text aloud. This helps users with visual impairments or reading difficulties. Accessibility Features Accessibility features help people with disabilities use ICT systems. A screen reader reads out text and menus for users who cannot see the screen. Sticky Keys lets a user press keyboard shortcuts one key at a time. A magnifier zooms into part of the screen. Speech recognition lets a user control a computer by speaking. Network Settings and User Permissions Network settings control how a device connects to a network. A network is a group of connected devices that share data. Administrators can set user permissions. User permissions decide what files or programs a person can access. Restricting permissions keeps data safe and stops unauthorised changes. Security Protocols Security protocols are rules that protect data on a system. Passwords stop unauthorised users from logging in. Firewalls block unwanted network traffic. A firewall is software or hardware that filters incoming and outgoing data. Encryption scrambles data so only authorised users can read it. These settings can be configured to match an organisation's security needs.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > ICT systems to meet specified needs

content.topicNotes: Tab Stops and Line Spacing Purpose of Tab Stops A tab stop is a predefined position where text aligns. Tab stops help users organise and align data. They create neat layouts without using multiple spaces. Tabulated text is text arranged using tab stops. Types of Tab Stops A left tab aligns text from the left edge of the tab stop. A right tab aligns text to the right edge of the tab stop. A centre tab centres text on the tab stop. A decimal tab aligns numbers by their decimal points. Tab Leaders A tab leader fills the blank space before a tab stop using repeated characters. Frequently used leader characters feature dot patterns (....), dashed lines (----), or continuous underlines (____). Tab leaders guide the reader's eye across pages in tables of contents, agendas, and menus by linking entries directly to page or price figures. Aligning Data Users align data to improve readability. Right tabs align values such as prices. Decimal tabs align numbers with decimal places. Consistent alignment makes information easier to compare. Indented Paragraphs An indented paragraph starts further from the margin. Users apply indentation to separate text from surrounding content. Indents improve document structure. Tab settings can help create consistent indentation. Line Spacing Line spacing is the vertical distance between lines of text in a document. It is set using software controls to adjust spacing to single, 1.5, or double lines. Proper spacing improves readability and leaves room for physical annotations or feedback. For example, essays often use 1.5 or double line spacing to make large blocks of text easier to read.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Word Processing
ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Word Processing

content.topicNotes: Tables in Web Pages Table Structure The <table> tag creates a table structure on a web page. A table organises data into rows and columns. Tables help users read and compare information. Web developers use tables for structured data rather than page layout. Rows and Cells The <tr> tag creates a table row. The <td> tag creates a table cell. A cell stores individual pieces of information. Rows and cells work together to organise data clearly. Captions and Borders The <caption> tag adds a title to a table. A caption explains the purpose of the table. Table borders separate cells visually. Borders make data easier to read and identify. Headers The <th> tag creates a table header. A header identifies the content of a row or column. Headers usually appear in bold and centre aligned by default. Headers improve readability and organisation. Table Sections The <thead> tag stores table headings. The <tbody> tag stores the main table data. The <tfoot> tag stores summary or footer information. These sections organise large tables and improve structure.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Software Skills > Web Authoring

content.topicNotes: Tablet and Phablet Computers What are tablets and phablets A tablet computer is a portable device with a flat touch screen and no built-in physical keyboard. A phablet is a device that is larger than a smartphone but smaller than a tablet. A phablet combines features of a phone and a tablet. Both devices use touch input as the main method of control. They run mobile operating systems designed for touch interaction. Uses of tablets and phablets Tablets are used for internet browsing, email and multimedia consumption. Students use tablets for reading digital textbooks and note-taking. Phablets are commonly used for communication and media on larger screens. Businesses use tablets for presentations and data collection. Both devices are used for gaming and educational apps. Tablets are used to remotely control devices e.g. smart home apps to adjust heating, flying drones etc. Advantages of tablets and phablets Tablets and phablets are lightweight and highly portable. Touch screens make them intuitive and easy to use. Battery life is usually longer than laptops. Built-in wireless connectivity allows mobile internet access. They start up quickly compared to traditional computers. Disadvantages of tablets and phablets Touch screen keyboards are slower for typing long documents. Limited processing power compared to desktops and laptops. Storage capacity is often smaller. Fewer professional software applications are available. Repairs and upgrades are usually not possible.
content.description: ICT: Edexcel International GCSE > Digital Devices > Types of Digital Devices

content.topicNotes: Targeted Marketing and Personalisation Techniques What is Targeted Marketing? Targeted marketing means showing adverts to specific groups of people. It is based on what those people are likely to want or buy. Online services collect data about users to do this. This makes adverts more relevant to each person. How Targeted Adverts Work Companies use your data to build a profile about you. A profile stores details like your age, interests and browsing habits. Algorithms then match adverts to your profile. An algorithm is a set of rules a computer follows to make decisions. You see adverts for things you are more likely to buy. Personalisation Techniques Personalisation means changing content to suit each user. Streaming services suggest films based on what you have watched. Online shops show products similar to ones you have looked at. News sites display stories based on topics you read before. Search engines rank results based on your past searches. Benefits of Targeted Marketing Users see adverts that match their interests. It can save time when searching for products. Businesses reach the right customers more easily. Online services can feel more useful and personal to each user. Concerns About Targeted Marketing Large amounts of personal data are collected without users always knowing. This raises privacy concerns. Filter bubbles can form. A filter bubble is when you only see content that matches your existing views. Some users feel their data is shared or sold without clear consent.

content.topicNotes: Web Authoring: Using a Template What is a Web Page Template? A template gives your website a consistent look across all pages. It has a set layout with placeholder areas for your own content. You replace the placeholder text and images with your own. Using a template saves time and keeps pages looking the same. Standard Page Features Most web page templates include a set of standard features. A header sits at the top and shows the site name or logo. A main content area holds the text and images for each page. A footer sits at the bottom and often shows contact details or copyright. These features appear on every page of the site. Banners A banner is a wide strip, usually at the top of the page. It often shows the website name, a logo, or a key image. Banners make a site easy to recognise. Templates include a banner area so every page looks the same. Menu and Navigation A menu (also called a navigation bar) links to other pages on the site. It helps visitors find what they need quickly. Menus can be horizontal (across the top) or vertical (down the side). Each link in the menu is called a hyperlink. A hyperlink is a clickable link that takes you to another page. Templates place the menu in the same spot on every page.

content.topicNotes: Text Alignment Left Alignment Left alignment places text evenly against the left margin. The right side of the text appears uneven. This is the default alignment in many documents. It is easy for users to read. Right Alignment Right alignment places text evenly against the right margin. The left side of the text appears uneven. It is often used for dates or headings. It can create a different visual effect in documents. Centre Alignment Centre alignment positions text equally between both margins. It is commonly used for titles and headings. This alignment draws attention to important text. Large amounts of centred text can reduce readability. Fully Justified Text Fully justified text is distributed evenly with both margins. The software adjusts spacing between words. This creates a neat and professional appearance. Uneven word spacing can sometimes make text harder to read. Choosing Alignment Different alignments suit different document purposes. Consistent alignment improves presentation. Users should choose alignment based on readability. Good formatting makes documents easier to understand.

content.topicNotes: Text Enhancement Bold, Italic and Underline Bold text makes important words stand out. Italic text slants characters to add emphasis. Underline places a line beneath text. Users apply these enhancements to improve document presentation. Highlighting Text Highlighting adds a coloured background behind text. Users highlight important information to attract attention. Highlighting makes key points easier to locate. Excessive highlighting can reduce its effectiveness and readability. Text Colour Text colour changes the appearance of characters. Users select colours to improve presentation or match a design. Good colour choices maintain readability. Poor colour contrast can make text difficult to read. Bulleted Lists A bulleted list uses symbols to separate items. Bulleted lists present related information without implying order. Users can create or edit bulleted lists. Bullets make information easier to read and scan. Numbered Lists A numbered list uses numbers to organise items. Numbered lists show a sequence or priority. Users create numbered lists for instructions or procedures. Numbering helps readers follow steps in the correct order.

content.topicNotes: Text Enhancement Bold, Italic and Underline Bold text appears darker and thicker than normal text. Italic text is slanted to the side. Underlined text has a line beneath it. These enhancements highlight important information. Paragraph Spacing Paragraph spacing controls the gaps before and after paragraphs. A paragraph is a section of related text. Extra spacing improves readability. Consistent spacing creates a neat document layout. When the last line of a paragraph appears isolated at the top of a new page it is called a widow. When the first line of a paragraph appears isolated at the bottom of a page it is called an orphan. Line Spacing Line spacing controls the vertical space between lines of text. Larger spacing can make text easier to read. Small spacing allows more text to fit on a page. Users should choose spacing suitable for the document purpose. Bullet Points Bullet points organise information into lists. Bullets can use different shapes such as circles or squares. Indent controls how far bullets are from the margin. Consistent alignment improves presentation. Using Formatting Effectively Too much enhancement can make text difficult to read. Consistent formatting improves document appearance. Bullets help users identify key points quickly. Good spacing makes information easier to understand.

content.topicNotes: Head Section and Metadata Page title The <title> tag defines the page title. The page title appears in the browser tab. It helps users identify the web page quickly. Each web page should have a clear, unique title. Meta tags overview Meta tags provide information about a web page. They are placed inside the <head> section. They are not displayed on the page itself. Search engines use meta tags to understand pages. Charset and author The charset defines character encoding using <meta charset="UTF-8">. UTF-8 allows most characters and symbols to display correctly. Author meta data identifies the creator of the page. This information is useful for documentation and ownership. Description and keywords A description meta tag summarises the web page content. Keywords help search engines identify page topics. Example: <meta name="description" content="ICT notes">. Keywords improve search engine visibility. Viewport settings The viewport controls how a page displays on different devices. It ensures content fits mobile and desktop screens. Example: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">. It helps make websites responsive.

content.topicNotes: Style Consistency What is a Style? A style is a set of formatting settings. Styles control fonts, colours and spacing. Users can apply styles to headings and text. Styles help documents to be more organised and consistent. Consistent Presentation Consistency means keeping the same appearance throughout a document. Styles ensure headings and paragraphs match. This improves readability for users. Creating and Modifying Styles Users can create custom styles for documents. A custom style is a user-defined formatting set. Existing styles can be modified when needed. Changes update all text using that style automatically. Applying Styles Styles can be applied to titles, headings and body text. Applying styles saves time when formatting. Users avoid changing each section individually. This reduces formatting errors in documents. Advantages of Styles Styles improve the appearance of documents. They make updates faster and easier. Consistent formatting helps users navigate information. Styles are useful in long or complex documents.

content.topicNotes: What are Headers and Footers? Headers & Footers Headers appear in the top margin of a document page. Margins are the blank spaces around the edges of a page. Footers appear in the bottom margin of a document page. Software duplicates the headers and footers' content automatically across multiple pages. Purpose of Headers & Footers Headers are typically used to display the document title, chapter name, or logos. Footers are used to display page numbers or the current date. Headers and footers save time and effort by applying the relevant information to all pages. Section breaks enable distinct headers, footers, restarted page counts, or custom margins within separate parts of one file. Practical exams typically ask students to place their credentials alongside an automated file name or path in the footer. Automated Fields Automated fields update their data dynamically without manual editing. Automated fields are placeholders that fetch live system information. Users insert automated fields to show the current date or total page count. Dynamic fields save time and prevent consistency errors across long reports.

content.topicNotes: Touch Screens & Graphics Tablets Touch screen A touch screen is an input and output device that detects touch on the display surface. Users interact by tapping, swiping or pinching the screen. Touch screens are commonly used on smartphones, tablets and kiosks. Touch input allows direct interaction with on-screen items. Uses of touch screens Touch screens are used in smartphones for apps and communication. ATMs and ticket machines use touch screens for public access. Tablets use touch screens for drawing and note-taking. Retail systems use touch screens at checkouts. Advantages and disadvantages a touch screen Advantages of a touch screen A touch screen is intuitive and easy to use. A touch screen does not require an additional pointing device. Touch screens reduce the need for separate keyboards and mice. Disadvantages of a touch screen A touch screen can become dirty or damaged. A touch screen may be less precise for detailed tasks. Graphics Tablets A graphics tablet is a flat input pad that registers strokes from a specialized stylus pen. Artists use these devices to sketch illustrations and edit digital photos with fine precision. Sensors track pen pressure and movement to alter line thickness on screen.

content.topicNotes: Transactional Data What is Transactional Data? Transactional data is information collected when a user does something online. Examples: buying a product, logging in, or searching for something. Every action a user takes can be recorded. This data helps businesses learn about their customers. What Gets Collected? Name and contact details are collected when you create an account. Payment details are stored when you buy something online. Your location may be recorded from your device. Items you view or buy are logged as purchase history. The date and time of each action are also saved. What Are Cookies? A cookie is a small file saved on your device by a website. It stores information about your visit. For example: items in your basket or your login details. When you return to the site, it reads the cookie. This lets the site remember you and your preferences. How Cookies Track You Third-party cookies track you across different websites. A third-party cookie is set by a site other than the one you are visiting. They build a profile of your browsing habits. Advertisers use this profile to show you targeted adverts. Targeted adverts match products to your interests. Transaction Tracking Transaction tracking records what users do during a visit. It logs which pages you view and for how long. It records what you search for and what you click. Businesses use this data to improve their websites. They also use it to recommend products you may want. How Businesses Use Transactional Data Businesses analyse transactional data to spot buying patterns. They use it to send personalised offers by email. Stock levels can be managed using purchase records. Data can be sold to other companies for marketing. This raises privacy concerns for users.

content.topicNotes: Two-Factor Authentication What is 2FA? Two-factor authentication (2FA) uses two methods to verify identity. It adds extra security beyond a password. Authentication is the process of confirming a user's identity. How 2FA Works Users enter a password as the first factor. A second factor is then required. There are different kinds of second factor. Most common is a code sent to a device. Access is only granted when both factors are correct. Types of Factors Something you know, for example, passwords or PINs (Personal Identification Number). Something you have, for example, a phone or a hardware token. Something you are and what makes you unique, for example, biometrics like fingerprints. Purpose of 2FA 2FA protects sensitive data and accounts. It makes it harder for attackers to gain access. Even if a password is stolen, access is still protected by the second factor. It is widely used in banking and online services.

content.topicNotes: Types of Data Text Data Text data is made up of letters, words and sentences. It is used to store names, addresses and descriptions. A contact list on a phone stores text data. Text data can also include symbols and punctuation. Numerical Data Numerical data is made up of numbers. It can be used in calculations. For example, adding up prices in a shop. There are two types of numerical data. Integers are whole numbers, such as 5 or 100. Real numbers include decimals, such as 3.14. Image Data Image data stores pictures and photographs. Digital images are made up of tiny dots called pixels. Each pixel stores colour information. Image data is used in social media, websites and documents. Examples include JPEG and PNG photo files. Sound Data Sound data stores audio, such as music or speech. Sound in the real world is analogue. Analogue means it changes smoothly and continuously. Computers store sound as digital data. Digital means it is stored as numbers (0s and 1s). An ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) changes analogue sound into digital data. Animation Data Animation data is a sequence of images shown quickly one after another. This creates the appearance of movement. Animations are used in games, videos and websites. Each image in an animation is called a frame.

content.topicNotes: Unequal Access to ICT What is Unequal Access to ICT? Unequal access to ICT means not everyone has access to digital technologies. Digital technologies include computers, the internet, and mobile devices. Some people have full access. Others have little or none. Causes of Unequal Access Cost is a major cause. Devices and internet connections can be expensive. Some areas lack the infrastructure needed. Infrastructure means cables, phone masts, and broadband networks. In rural or remote areas, connections are often slow or missing. Age can be a barrier. Older people may find technology hard to learn. Disability can also limit access if devices are not adapted. Causes of Unequal Access (continued) Education is a cause. People with fewer digital skills use ICT less. Digital skills mean knowing how to use a computer or the internet. Language can be a barrier. Most online content is in a few languages. Government policy matters. Some countries restrict internet use. Gender can play a role in some regions, where women have less access. Impact on Individuals People without access cannot use online banking or shopping. They miss out on online education and e-learning resources. Finding jobs is harder. Many employers only advertise roles online. Healthcare information and services are often only available online. Social isolation can grow when people cannot communicate digitally. Impact on Communities Communities with poor access fall behind economically. Local businesses cannot compete with online-only competitors. Public services are harder to reach if they move online. Schools without ICT resources produce students with fewer digital skills. Whole regions can be left out of the modern digital economy. Local and Global Perspectives Locally, poorer areas in a country often have slower or no broadband. Globally, developing countries have far fewer internet users per person. In some countries, fewer than one in ten people are online. This widens the gap in education, health, and wealth between nations. Closing the digital divide is a key global challenge.

content.topicNotes: Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) What is a VPN? A VPN (Virtual Private Network) is a secure, private connection over the internet. It lets a device connect to another network as if it were directly plugged in. Data sent through a VPN is encrypted (scrambled so others cannot read it). This keeps the connection private, even on a public network. How a VPN Works A VPN creates a 'tunnel' between two devices or networks. A tunnel is an encrypted path that hides the data inside it. Data travels through this tunnel across the internet. Anyone who intercepts the data cannot read it without the encryption key. Why VPNs Are Used VPNs keep data safe when using public Wi-Fi, such as in a cafe. They let employees access a company's private network from home. Businesses use VPNs to protect sensitive data sent between offices. VPNs also hide a user's IP address, adding extra privacy. VPNs in the Workplace A remote worker can use a VPN to connect securely to their company's network. They can access files and systems as if they were in the office. The company's data stays protected because the connection is encrypted. This reduces the risk of data being stolen by hackers. Benefits and Limitations of VPNs Benefits: Data is encrypted. Identity is hidden. Remote access is possible. Limitations: VPN can slow down the connection speed. VPNs require software and setup, which can be complex for some users.

content.topicNotes: Validation Checks Purpose of Validation Validation is the process of checking data against pre-defined rules before processing. Validation checks ensure entered data is sensible. It helps reduce data entry errors and therefore improves data quality and reliability. Range and Character Checks A range check ensures data falls between set limits.For example, a test score must be between 0 and 100. A character check ensures only allowed characters are entered. For example, a name should not contain numbers. Length and Type Checks A length check ensures data contains the correct number of characters.A password may require at least eight characters. A type check ensures the correct data type is entered.For example, an age field should contain numbers. Format and Presence Checks A format check ensures data follows a required pattern.An email address must follow a valid email format. A presence check ensures a field is not left blank. Required fields must contain data before submission. Importance of Validation Validation helps prevent incorrect data from being stored. It reduces the need to correct errors later. Validation does not guarantee data is accurate. It only checks whether data meets defined rules.

content.topicNotes: WEP and WPA Why Wireless Networks Need Security A wireless network sends data through the air using radio waves. Anyone nearby could intercept that data without the right protection. Encryption is used to scramble data so only the intended receiver can read it. Encryption turns readable data into a coded form. WEP and WPA are two encryption standards used to protect wireless networks. WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) WEP stands for Wired Equivalent Privacy. It was introduced in 1997 as the first wireless encryption standard. WEP uses a shared key (a password) to encrypt data on a Wi-Fi network. WEP is now considered weak and insecure. Attackers can crack a WEP key in minutes using freely available tools. WEP should not be used on modern networks. WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) WPA stands for Wi-Fi Protected Access. It was introduced in 2003 to replace WEP. WPA uses stronger encryption and changes the encryption key automatically. This makes it much harder to crack than WEP. WPA2 followed in 2004 and is now the most widely used standard. WPA3 is the latest version, offering even stronger protection. Key Differences: WEP vs WPA WEP uses a fixed, static encryption key. The same key is used every time, making it easy to crack. WPA uses a dynamic key that changes regularly. This makes intercepted data much harder to decode. WPA also checks data has not been tampered with during transmission. WPA is far more secure than WEP.

content.topicNotes: Wi-Fi What Wi-Fi Is Wi-Fi stands for Wireless Fidelity Wi-Fi is a wireless technology that connects devices to a network. It uses radio waves instead of cables. A Wi-Fi router provides the wireless signal. How Wi-Fi Works Devices connect to a wireless access point to join a Wi-Fi network. The access point sends and receives data using radio signals with several different frequencies. The most common frequencies are 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz, where a connection with 5 GHz is faster but has less range. Wi-Fi networks use SSIDs to identify the network name. SSID stands for Service Set Identifier. Advantages of Wi-Fi Wi-Fi provides high data transmission speeds, making it ideal for streaming high-definition video and sharing large files. Wi-Fi allows devices to move around without cables. It supports many devices in homes and schools. It makes it easy to connect laptops and phones. It is suitable for general internet use. Limitations of Wi-Fi Wi-Fi signals can be weaker through walls and floors. The connection can slow down with many users. Interference from other devices can reduce speed. Wi-Fi is less secure if it uses weak passwords.

content.topicNotes: Working From Home What is Working From Home? Working from home means doing your job from your house instead of an office. Digital devices and an internet connection make this possible. The internet connects workers to colleagues, files and systems from any location. This style of work is sometimes called remote working. How Technology Enables Working From Home Laptops and tablets let workers use software away from the office. A broadband internet connection links the worker to their organisation's network. Video calling tools, e.g. Zoom, allow face-to-face meetings online. Cloud storage lets workers access and share files from any device. Cloud storage means files are held on remote servers, not just one machine. Email and messaging apps keep teams in contact throughout the day. Benefits for Individuals Workers save time and money by not commuting. They can set up their own workspace to suit their needs. Working from home can improve work-life balance. It gives more flexibility over working hours in some jobs. Workers with disabilities or caring responsibilities may find this option easier. Drawbacks for Individuals Workers may feel isolated without face-to-face contact. Home distractions, e.g. family or noise, can reduce focus. The boundary between work and home life can blur. Not every home has a fast enough internet connection. Some workers miss out on in-person training or mentoring. Benefits for Organisations Organisations can reduce costs by needing less office space. They can hire workers from a wider geographical area. Staff may be more productive when working in a comfortable environment. Fewer workers on site can lower heating, lighting and facilities costs. Offering remote work can help attract and keep skilled staff. Drawbacks for Organisations It is harder to monitor staff performance and output remotely. Sharing data over the internet raises security risks. Team collaboration can be more difficult without in-person meetings. The organisation may need to fund equipment for home workers. Technical problems at home can disrupt work and reduce productivity.

content.topicNotes: Wrapping Text Around Images Text Wrap Basics Users apply text wrapping to control how document text flows around an inserted graphic. Text Wrapping: a feature that allows text to surround an image rather than treating the image as a single large character. Designers use this to integrate images naturally within paragraphs of a report or newsletter. This technique ensures that there is no large, awkward white space around the image area. Common Wrapping Styles - Part 1 In line with text: treats the image like a piece of text within the sentence or paragraph. Square: forces the text to flow around the rectangular border of the image frame. Tight: allows the text to follow the actual contours or outline of the image. Contours: the outer edges or shape of an object. Through: enables text to flow into any open white space or gaps within the image itself. Common Wrapping Styles - Part 2 Top and Bottom: places text only above and below the graphic, leaving the sides empty. Behind text: positions the image on a layer underneath the words so they overlap the graphic. Behind text is useful to set a background image in a document. In front of text: places the image on the top layer so it covers any text behind it.
